text: What FlowCHAOS is, what it models, and how a study runs from the first line to the last report.

FlowCHAOS (Comprehensive Hydraulic Analysis & Optimization System) is a Windows program for the design and analysis of pressurised water networks: town and city supplies, rural gravity schemes, bulk transfer mains, building plumbing and irrigation systems. It brings into one model the steps an engineer usually spreads over several programs: drawing the network on real maps, with survey points, scanned drawings, satellite imagery and ground levels; the hydraulic and water quality analysis of the network, at one moment or through days of use; the design tools that size pipes, check fire flow, find critical mains and lay out irrigation; the quantities, costs and construction programme that follow from the design; map sheets, profiles, reports and animations that present it. Because every step works on the same model, the network that is analysed is the network that is priced, drawn and built.

A network model describes a water system as nodes joined by links: nodes are the points where water enters, leaves or is stored: junctions (where pipes meet and water is taken), reservoirs (sources with a fixed water level, such as a lake, a river intake or a bulk supply) and tanks (storage whose level rises and falls); links carry water between nodes: pipes, pumps and valves. Each element carries the data the physics needs: ground and hydraulic levels and withdrawals at the junctions; lengths, diameters and roughness of the pipes; curves of the pumps; types and settings of the valves; sizes and levels of the tanks. Around them sit the data that describe time: demand profiles (how use varies through the day), curves (pump head, efficiency, tank volume, head loss), controls and rules (when pumps, pipes and valves change).

For a moment in time (a steady state) or a sequence of moments (an extended period), the analysis finds: the flow and velocity in every pipe, pump and valve, and the direction the water moves; the head (the level water would rise to in a standpipe) and the pressure at every node; the water delivered at each junction, which can be less than the design withdrawal when the pressure is too low (pressure-driven analysis); the level of every tank, the status of every pump and valve, and the energy used by pumping and its cost; the water quality: the concentration of chlorine or another substance, the age of the water, or the share of water coming from a chosen source, everywhere in the network.

Hydraulics Water quality Networks of any size and layout, branched or looped Movement of a substance with the flow, mixing at junctions Friction by Hazen-Williams, Darcy-Weisbach or Chezy-Manning Reactions in the water (bulk) and at the pipe walls, first or higher order Minor losses at bends and fittings Limiting concentrations (a reaction stops at a level) Fixed-speed and variable-speed pumps, with their curves Four ways tanks can mix their water Pressure reducing, sustaining and breaking valves, flow control, throttle control and general valves with their own loss curves Sources at any node: inflow concentration, boosters, flow-paced dosing, mass injection Check valves and pipes that can be opened or closed Water age and source tracing Tanks of any shape (with a volume curve) Sources that act for part of a run (an intrusion) Demands that vary in time, several categories at a junction Compliance against limits, by node and by delivered water Demand-driven or pressure-driven withdrawal, emitters for leaks and sprinklers Controls on time, clock time, tank level and pressure, and rules with AND, OR, ELSE and priorities

A typical study follows these steps; each has a chapter in this manual. Set up the project with its coordinate system and units (Working with projects). Bring in the ground and the existing data: basemaps, a DEM, survey points, drawings, older models (Layers and data). Draw or import the network and give its elements their properties (Drawing and editing, The network model). Describe time: demand profiles, pump and tank curves, controls and rules (Controls and rules). Choose the analysis options (Analysis options) and run (Running an analysis). Read the results on the map, in tables and graphs, and fix what does not meet the design criteria (Reading the results, Map views). Design: size the pipes, check fire flow and critical mains, plan irrigation (Design tools). Check the water quality (Water quality). Deliver: quantities, construction programme, map sheets and reports (Quantities and planning, Map sheets and reports).

FlowCHAOS is made for water and irrigation engineers, consultants, water utilities and boards, contractors, plumbers, lecturers and students. A network of a few pipes and one of many thousands are handled the same way; large networks draw quickly (labels and symbols are simplified on their own when there are many elements) and long work, such as runs, contours and DEMs, happens in the background with its progress in the status bar, while the window stays usable.

Menu commands are written as Menu > Command, for example Analysis > Water Quality Analysis. Buttons, fields and tabs are written in bold, as they appear on the screen. Lengths and levels are in metres, pressures and heads in metres of water, flows in litres per second unless the project uses other units (Units of measurement). A worked example is set out as numbered steps; tips and cautions follow the text they belong to.
Put FlowCHAOS on your computer with its installer.

System Windows 10 or later, 64-bit (Windows 10 or 11 recommended) Memory 4 GB (8 GB for large networks and terrain) Disk 1 GB Internet only for basemaps, satellite imagery, place search and online terrain

Download the installer from the download page. Each file is listed with its SHA-256 checksum so you can verify it: certutil -hashfile FlowCHAOS-Setup.exe SHA256 must give the same value. There are two kinds: Setup (EXE) for one computer: a guided setup that adds FlowCHAOS to the Start menu and opens imported hydraulic model input files (.inp) with it. Installer (MSI) for organisations: installs for every user and can be deployed silently: msiexec /i FlowCHAOS-x64.msi /qn.

Install a newer version over the old one; your settings and plugins are kept. Remove FlowCHAOS from Settings > Apps in Windows. The setup program then asks whether to remove your settings, the map tile cache, logs, reference data and plugins too: choose Yes for a clean start, No to keep them for a reinstall. A silent uninstall keeps them unless /PURGE=yes is given. Your projects are ordinary files and stay where you saved them.
What Where Your plugins %USERPROFILE%\.flowchaos\plugins Your own reference data %APPDATA%\FlowCHAOS\data The log (for bug reports) %LOCALAPPDATA%\FlowCHAOS\FlowCHAOS\logs\flowchaos.log

A worked example: a village supply from a spring, drawn, analysed, improved and reported, step by step. This tutorial builds a small gravity scheme: a protected spring feeds a storage tank, which supplies four communal taps. It takes about forty minutes and touches every main part of FlowCHAOS. The values are typical of a rural scheme in Malawi; use your own when you repeat it for a real site.

File > New. The project uses UTM zone 36 South (EPSG:32736); for a site in another zone, click the coordinate system in the status bar and choose yours. File > Project Properties > General: name the project "Village supply tutorial". Press the satellite button on the toolbar and choose a satellite basemap to see the ground. Go to your site with View > Go to Coordinates, or with the place search on the toolbar. Analysis > Analysis Options > Hydraulics: flow units L/s, head loss formula Hazen-Williams. Leave the rest as it is.

The network is drawn in a network layer; the first drawing tool creates one and starts editing it. Choose Reservoir on the drawing toolbar and click where the spring is. In Element Properties set its Total Head to the level of the spring's water surface, for example 1148 m. Name it Spring. Choose Tank and click about 850 m below the spring. Set its ground elevation (from the DEM, or type 1132 m), diameter 4.0 m, minimum level 0.3 m, maximum level 2.5 m and starting level 1.5 m. Name it Tank. Choose Pipe, click the spring, then the tank: the pipe follows your clicks; each click on empty ground places a bend. Double-click, Enter or right-click to finish. From the tank draw the distribution main to a junction J1, 420 m away, then branches to four taps, Tap1 to Tap4, 200 to 350 m from J1. Type a length (for example 260) and press Enter to place a point exactly that far. Select the four taps (Ctrl+click) and in Element Properties give them a design withdrawal of 0.15 L/s each (about 13 m3 a day per tap: some 500 people at 25 litres a day). Ground levels come from a DEM or online terrain automatically (Layer > Ground Elevation Source); check them in Element Properties, and type corrections where you surveyed.

Select the spring-to-tank pipe: material HDPE PE100, internal diameter 79 mm (the 90 mm PN10 pipe), roughness C 150. Select the distribution pipes with a box (drag across them): main 63 mm pipe (internal about 55 mm), branches 50 mm (internal about 44 mm). The material also feeds the bill of quantities. Select by Attribute (on the toolbar and the map's right-click menu) selects elements by any property, to change many at once.

Press Run Steady-State (F5). The Simulation Results panel opens and the nodes are coloured by pressure, with a legend on the map. Click Tap4: Element Properties shows its head, pressure and delivered withdrawal. In Map Styles, under Links, choose Velocity: the pipes are coloured too. Open Analysis > Solver Warnings: it should be empty. If not, see Errors and warnings. Check the pressures: at a communal tap, 5 to 10 m is comfortable; much more wastes water and wears taps, much less gives a weak flow.

section: 5. Make it move through the day
text: Communal taps are busy at dawn and late afternoon and closed at night. Analysis > Demand Profiles. Press New Profile, name it TAP, then from Preset choose the communal water point shape. The chart shows the multiplier for each hour. Select the taps and set their demand profile to TAP. Analysis > Analysis Options > Times: duration 48:00, hydraulic timestep 1:00. Analysis > Run Extended Period. The time bar of the Simulation Results panel now steps through 48 hours: press play to watch the tank level and the tap pressures change. Analysis > Advanced Graphs, Time Series of Tank, Level. A healthy tank fills at night and drains in the day without emptying.

If the tank overflows at night, close the inlet when it is full: Analysis > Scheduled Pipe Controls, Start from a Sample, Close the tank inlet before it overflows. The sample is written with your tank and its inlet pipe; adjust the levels if needed. Run the extended period again and look at the tank's level graph.

Analysis > Water Quality Analysis, choose Chlorine residual compliance. The spring is the source at 1 mg/L; set the bulk rate from a bottle test if you have one. Press Run Water Quality Analysis. The summary says whether every tap keeps at least 0.2 mg/L. Show on Map and play the time bar to watch the chlorine travel.

Analysis > Automatic Pipe Sizing: pipe series HDPE PE100 PN10 (SDR 17), maximum velocity 1.5 m/s, minimum pressure 5 m, peak factor 1.0 (the profile already holds the peaks). Size Pipes. The table lists the size chosen for each pipe; Apply Sizes writes them into the network (Undo takes them back).

Select the pipes from the spring to Tap4 and choose Edit > Longitudinal Profile: the ground, the pipe and the hydraulic grade line along them. File > Export > Bill of Quantities: pipes by size and material, fittings, tanks and earthworks, priced from your rates. File > Export > Print Layout: a map sheet with the network, the legend, a scale bar, a north arrow and a title block, exported to PDF.

File > Save writes the project with everything: the network, results, styles, layouts and plans. A green bar confirms it. Every step can still be undone with Ctrl+Z. Next: the window, drawing and editing and the network model.
A tour of the window: where everything is and how it fits together.

The map in the middle shows everything you draw and import, over imagery, terrain or a plain background. Scroll to zoom, drag with the middle button (or the pan tool) to move, and use Ctrl+0 to see the whole network. Ctrl+Left and Ctrl+Right step back and forward through the views you have had.

File and edit: new, open, save, print, undo and redo. Navigate: select, pan and the zoom tools. Draw: junction, reservoir, tank, pipe, pump and valve. The small arrow beside pipe and pump tools chooses how they draw. Drafting: snap, ortho, the grid and measure. Modify: move, copy, rotate, scale, mirror, offset, split, divide, trim and extend. Run (first on the second row): steady-state and extended-period analysis, Animate Map, Stop / Clear Results, the Simulation Results panel and the Map Styles panel. Digitizing: editing of vector layers (add, select, move and delete features). Analysis and design: profiles, quantities, planning, surface maps and the design tools. Map and data: basemaps and satellite imagery, map options and layers. A command is available only when it can act: Export Results needs results, Rotate needs a selection. Point at a greyed command to see what it needs.

Layers (left): Networks, Vector layers, reference images, rasters, basemaps and surface maps, each group with its layers. The toolbar above the list adds every kind of layer, removes, opens properties and zooms. Double-click a layer for its properties (a 3D surface opens its 3D view). Element Properties (right): the values of what you select, ready to edit. The fields fit the panel and widen with it. Map Styles (right, at any time): what nodes and links are coloured by, each with its colour band and legend. A newly opened project shows each layer in its own colour until you choose a view. Simulation Results (bottom, after a run): the time bar, playback and the result tables. Value Relay (right): the source and destinations of Value Relay and its history. Log Messages (bottom): what the program reports, in tabs: all, messages, analysis, tasks, plugins, online and program. The button at the right of the status bar opens it and counts new warnings. Measure (under Element Properties, while measuring): the values of the measurement. Esc clears the measurement and leaves the tool. Panels on the same side share it as tabs (Element Properties, Map Styles and the Processing Toolbox on the right; Layers and Plugins on the left), so each keeps its full height. Drag a tab to move a panel, or out of the window to float it; View brings closed panels back. Each start shows the Layers, Element Properties and Map Styles panels and every toolbar again, in the places you left them.

From left to right: the cursor coordinates, the length and angle being drawn, two drawing aids (polar tracking and dynamic input), the network size, the coordinate system (click it for the project's coordinates), the map scale (pick or type 1:N) and the units of lengths. Toolbar buttons show their name in bold, the keyboard shortcut beside it and a short description below; a button that cannot be used yet adds what it needs. Every save and export confirms itself in a bar over the bottom of the window: green when the file was written, red when it could not be, with the reason and a Details button. The bar closes by itself; point at it to keep it open.

Big tools open in their own windows beside the map so you can keep working: print layouts, the planner, graphs, the attribute table, profiles, quantities, the georeferencer, 3D views, pipe sizing and fire flow. Every window fits the screen and keeps its buttons reachable.
FlowCHAOS starts in the light theme. Settings > Theme switches between light, dark and the system setting.

The first time FlowCHAOS starts, a short tour points out the map, the layers, the drawing and run buttons, map styles, results and the design tools. Use Next and Back (or the arrow keys), and Esc to close it. Start it again at any time from Help > Quick Tour.

Help > User Manual opens the full FlowCHAOS User Manual (PDF) in your PDF reader; it is installed with the program, so it works offline. Help > Help Contents (F1) opens this documentation inside FlowCHAOS, with search, also offline. The Help menu also has Getting Started, Keyboard Shortcuts, What's New, Report an Issue, Get Involved, Support and Contact, the FlowCHAOS home page and Check for Updates.

View > Processing Toolbox lists ready-made network tools in groups, each with its icon: network data (lengths from the drawing, missing sizes, roughness by material, renaming in order), topology and geometry (merging and snapping nodes, splitting and joining pipes, simplifying bends), checks (the whole network, disconnected parts, parallel and short pipes), demand (sharing a total, from population, scaling), analysis and design windows, terrain, irrigation, and reports and export, and five groups for vector layers (analysis, geoprocessing, geometry, selection and research, data management; see Vector layers under Data). Double-click a tool: its window has the parameters, a help page, and after Run a log and a table you can copy; elements it finds are selected on the map, and a change it makes is one step you can undo. Tools that cannot run yet are greyed with the reason in their tooltip. Plugins can add tools.
Projects and files: starting, opening, saving and setting up a project, and the defaults it uses.

A FlowCHAOS project (a .fchaos file) holds the whole work: every network layer, vector layer, raster and basemap; surface maps and contours; the analysis options, demand profiles, curves, controls and rules; the last results; labels, legends and map styles; print layouts; bills of quantities and construction plans; and the project's own settings. One file is everything another engineer needs to open the work where you left it. A network file (.fcnet) holds a single network, to share it or to add it to another project as a layer. FlowCHAOS also imports and exports hydraulic model input files (.inp), the format of the widely used public-domain network modelling program, so models can move between programs. It is not a FlowCHAOS format: FlowCHAOS's own files are the project (.fchaos) and the network file (.fcnet) (File formats).

File > New starts an empty project in UTM zone 36 South (EPSG:32736). Change the coordinate system in Project Properties > Coordinates, or click it in the status bar. File > Open opens a project, or starts a new project holding a network file as its first layer (.fcnet, .inp, .net, CSV, shapefile, KML, GPX, DXF). File > Open Recent lists the last projects opened. File > Open Sample Projects opens ready networks by discipline: town supply, rural gravity scheme, bulk transfer, chlorine study, building plumbing, georeferencing practice, and irrigation schemes from a 1.5 ha smallholder drip system to a 10 ha banana farm and a 50 ha centre pivot. Files can also be dragged onto the map: a project opens, other files are added as layers.

File > Save (Ctrl+S) writes the project; File > Save As writes it under another name. The title bar shows an asterisk while there are unsaved changes, and FlowCHAOS asks before closing or opening another project. Every save shows a green bar over the bottom of the window, or a red one with the reason if the file could not be written. Results are saved with the project, so a project reopens with its results on the map. Auto-save and recovery. While you work, FlowCHAOS writes a recovery copy of the project with its unsaved changes every few minutes (Settings > Auto-save: off, or every 1 to 30 minutes; 5 by default). The copy is kept in FlowCHAOS's own folder, never over your file, and is removed when the project is saved or FlowCHAOS closes normally. If FlowCHAOS stops unexpectedly, the next start offers to Recover the work: it opens as an unsaved project with its own file name, so Save puts it back.
Every change, from moving a node to applying pipe sizes, is one step of Edit > Undo (Ctrl+Z) and Edit > Redo (Ctrl+Y). The history covers the session; saving does not clear it.

File > Project Properties sets what applies to the whole project: Tab What it sets General the project name, title and description, the file, a summary of the network and its flow units Metadata author, organisation, keywords and an abstract, kept with the project and used in reports Coordinates the project's coordinate system (CRS), with its details Measurements how coordinates are shown (metres, degrees and minutes) and their decimals; units of lengths, areas and angles View the predefined map scales and how the map draws Data Sources the files the project's layers come from Elevation where ground levels come from: a DEM, online terrain, or typed values Analysis the head loss formula, demand model, duration and time step of runs, and the design standard The design standard sets the starting values of pipe sizing, fire flow, criticality and the withdrawal tools: water use per person, peak factor, losses, minimum and maximum pressure, velocity limits and fire flow. The presets describe typical schemes; check them against the standard that applies to your project, and add your own to design/standards.json in the reference data.

Every project has a coordinate system, and every layer keeps its own: a shapefile in geographic coordinates and a DXF in a local grid are each shown in the project's system without changing the files. Lengths of pipes are true ground lengths in that system. See Coordinates and units.

Settings > ID Labels and Element Defaults sets the names of new elements and the properties they are drawn with (see Analysis options). Draw quickly with sensible defaults, then correct what differs with Select by Attribute and the attribute table.

Window layouts, recent files, colour ramps, the language and similar preferences are kept for your Windows account, not in the project. Settings > Language and Region chooses the language of the menus and the number formats. Reference data you add (pipe series, standards, rates, curves) goes in %APPDATA%\FlowCHAOS\data and overrides the data installed with the program.
Draw pipes, nodes, pumps and valves precisely, then move, copy, rotate, scale and mirror them.

Choose the pipe tool and click to place nodes; every click adds a bend or a node depending on the pipe mode (the arrow beside the tool). While drawing, type to enter values exactly: Type Meaning 25 25 m towards the cursor 25<30 25 m at 30 degrees @10,-5 10 m east and 5 m south of the last point 500200,8501300 an absolute coordinate Press Enter to accept and Esc to stop. A typed length is kept exactly: a pipe drawn as 1000 is 1000 m long, also when it is finished with a double-click.

On the drafting toolbar: Snap: to nodes, pipes and the grid. Snapping to a pipe splits it when you place a node. With snapping off, a point goes exactly where you click and the grid is ignored, but a click right on a node or a pipe still lands on it, so a pipe never starts beside a node or doubles it. Ortho: horizontal and vertical segments only. Grid: the drawing grid (hidden under basemaps). In the status bar: Polar tracking: segments lock to every 15 degrees when you are near one. Dynamic input: length and angle in a small box beside the cursor while you draw or move.

With Select, drag a node to move it; its pipes follow, and a bend that sat on the node's old place goes with it. Drop the node on another node and the two become one, with all their pipes; drop it on a pipe (snapping on) and the pipe is split there and joined to the node. A click without a drag only selects. Click an empty place on the map to clear the selection. Changes go into the network layer being edited. If no layer is being edited, the first change starts editing the layer it is in. If another layer is being edited, nothing changes, the map shows the network as it is, and the status bar says which layer to edit (right-click it, Toggle Editing).

Select elements, then use the Modify toolbar or right-click on the map. The button of the tool in use stays pressed; Esc stops it and returns to Select. Move: pick a base point, then the destination (or type a distance). Clicking an element that is not selected moves that element alone. Copy with Base Point: as many copies as you click; Esc ends. Rotate: pick the centre, then the angle. Press R for a reference angle, C to rotate a copy. Scale: pick the fixed point, then the factor. R makes a length exactly so long; C scales a copy. Mirror: two points of the mirror line; the original stays unless you press E. Offset, Split and Divide for the selected pipe. Trim: hover over a pipe and the piece between bends, crossings and nodes turns red; click to remove it. Extend: hover near the end of a pipe and a green line shows how far it goes straight on to the next pipe; click to extend it. That pipe is split where they meet and joined to it. A free end moves there; an end that has other pipes stays, and a new pipe continues from it. Edit > Connect Link End to Node: with one link and one node selected, the end of the link nearer the node moves onto it. Edit > Dissolve Nodes: junctions that join two pipes are removed and the pipes become one line, so four nodes joined by three pipes become one pipe between the two outer nodes. It works on the selected nodes, on the nodes inside the selected pipes, or on every junction of the network. By default only pipes of the same diameter, roughness and material are joined and junctions with a withdrawal stay; you can also share a withdrawal between the two ends. The removed nodes become bends unless you ask for a straight line. Also on the right-click menu. Edit > Pipe Shape: Reverse Direction swaps the ends of the selected links; Simplify Shape removes bends that hardly change the line (closer than the distance you give to a straighter line); Fillet Bends turns every bend into a smooth curve of the radius you give (polyethylene is laid to about 25 times its diameter); Set Exact Length moves the free end of the selected pipe along its last straight piece until the pipe is exactly so long. Select by Region and Delete by Region (Edit menu, or the arrow beside the Select button): click the corners of an area, double-click or press Enter to close it, and everything inside is selected or deleted. Right-click removes the last corner, Esc stops. Every step shows a preview before you click and can be undone.

Edit > Value Relay (Shift+V) passes a property from one element to others. Choose the property (diameter, roughness, withdrawal, ground level, pressure class, material and others) and whether to copy it (the source keeps its value) or move it (the source is set to zero or emptied). Click the source: it is marked SOURCE in red. Then click a destination of the same kind: it takes the value at once and is marked DESTINATION in green. Pick the next pair the same way; Enter or Esc asks whether to leave the tool. Every transfer is one step to undo.

Edit > Convert To (or right-click the selection) changes the type of the selected elements without drawing them again: junctions, reservoirs and tanks become one another; the place, ground level, layer, labels and your own fields are kept, and what only the new type has takes the element defaults; a junction between two pipes becomes a pump or a valve: it is split in two and the pump or valve is put between the halves; pipes, pumps and valves become one another. A name made from the old type's prefix (J12) takes the next name of the new type (R1), and controls and rules follow the new name. New projects show the IDs of nodes and pipes from the start.

Settings > ID Labels and Element Defaults sets how new elements are named and what they are given: ID Labels: a prefix for junctions, reservoirs, tanks, pipes, pumps and valves (J, R, T, P, PU and V by default), the first number and the increment (10 gives J10, J20, J30). The page shows the next names. Element Defaults: ground elevation (used where no elevation model or survey gives one), the design offset and withdrawal of junctions, their demand profile and emitter coefficient; tank stand height, diameter and levels; pipe diameter, roughness and minor loss; and the type of new valves. The settings are kept with the project.

The Edit menu has tools that save hours on a large design (also on the map's right-click menu when pipes are selected): Insert Components on Pipes: one component on every selected pipe: an isolation valve, a pressure reducing or sustaining valve, a flow control or pressure breaker valve, a check valve, a meter or a pump. Choose where: at the start or the end of each pipe as drawn, at its upstream or downstream end (by the flows of the last run), or in its middle. The component takes a short piece of the pipe (0.5 m by default) next to a new junction, so the pipe keeps its name, layer and properties. For example: select every tertiary pipe with Select by Attribute (diameter below 63 mm), then insert isolation valves at their upstream ends, named IV1, IV2 and so on. Mark High and Low Points: along the selected pipes, an air valve at every junction higher than its neighbours and a washout at every one lower than them, ready for the bill of quantities. Connect Points to Nearest Pipe: a service pipe from each selected unconnected node (a house, a tap, a hydrant) to the nearest pipe, which is split at the tee. Each is one step of Undo.

Drag left to right for a window selection (whole elements), right to left for a crossing selection. Select Similar, Select Connected Network and Select by Attribute (on the toolbar and the map's right-click menu) select by rule. Selected elements are drawn in the selection colour with a halo that stays the same size at every zoom. View > Map Options > Selection sets the colour, turns the halo off, or makes it pulse so a selected node is easy to find on a busy map.
Bring in networks, survey points, drawings, rasters and basemaps, each in its own coordinate system.

Use the Add Layer button above the layers list (or drag files onto the map): Network layer: FlowCHAOS network files (.fcnet), hydraulic model files (.inp, .net), network CSV, shapefiles and KML. Survey points: XYZ, CSV, TXT and spreadsheet files. Points become unconnected nodes with their ground level and every column of the file, ready to label and contour. Raster or DEM: GeoTIFF and other rasters. A DEM can supply ground levels. A PDF drawing or map comes in as an image: choose its page (see Georeferencing below). Vector layer from file (Ctrl+Shift+V): shapefiles, GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KML and DXF drawings as vector layers, every layer and kind of geometry of the file. CAD drawing (DXF): lines, polylines, arcs and splines become a network (see below), or the whole drawing comes in as vector layers (see DXF drawings as vector layers). Surface map: contours and other maps from points or a DEM. Satellite and basemaps: online imagery, street and topographic maps, vector basemaps, your own tile services and offline tile packages.

Every network is a layer, listed under Networks in the Layers panel: the network of a new project, networks added with Add Layer or File > Import Network > Hydraulic Model, a file dropped on the map, a file opened with File > Open (a new project holding it as its first layer), survey points, and empty layers made with Layer > Add Empty Network Layer. A layer brings everything it needs to run: curves, demand profiles, controls and rules come with it, and names already used in the project are renamed (T1 becomes T1_2) together with every reference to them. The first layer of an empty project also sets the analysis options, times, energy and report settings. A network layer is changed only while it is being edited, as in a GIS: right-click it and choose Toggle Editing (its name turns bold, with a pencil). What you draw goes into that layer, a new pipe connects only to its nodes, and the other layers stay as they are; an attempt to change them says which layer to edit. Choosing a drawing tool starts editing by itself when it is clear which layer: the only one, or a new one in an empty project; with several layers FlowCHAOS asks. Right-click a network layer for its menu: Toggle Editing, Zoom to Layer, Attribute Table, labels, Analyse This Network, Export Layer As (FlowCHAOS network, hydraulic model, CSV, GeoJSON, shapefile, GeoPackage, KML or DXF of that layer alone), Rename, Properties and Remove. Right-clicking an element on the map shows the same commands for its layer, under Layer. A FlowCHAOS network file (.fcnet) holds one network with every property, the profiles, curves, controls and rules it uses, its coordinate system and its look (symbol and labels). Use it to share a network or to add it to another project as a layer; a project file (.fchaos) holds the whole work. Properties of a network layer has, on its Information page, Show on map switches: junction nodes, tanks and sources, pipes, pumps and valves, and labels. Hiding the junctions shows the pipes alone on a dense network; the hidden elements stay in the network and in the analysis. Hide a layer and its elements leave the map and the analysis; its labels, colours and attribute table are its own (labels follow Map Options until the layer is given its own). After a run the map shows the network that was analysed. A progress window shows each stage of a long import; what was imported, and any notes, go to the status bar and the log. A message box opens only when something needs your attention.

section: Networks from lines (DXF, shapefiles, KML, GPX)
text: Lines become pipes and their ends become junctions. A junction is placed only where pipes meet: at the ends of lines, where lines join end to end, and at a tee, where the end of one line lies on another, which is then split there. Bends stay as vertices of a pipe, so a curved main is one pipe with its true length, not a chain of short pipes. Two pipes that meet end to end with the same diameter, roughness and drawing layer are joined into one. Point features become junctions with their elevation and withdrawal when the file has them. From a DXF, lines, polylines, 3D polylines, arcs, splines and ellipses are read. The drawing layer of each line is kept as a field; a diameter in the layer name (DN150, D110, 160mm) becomes the pipe diameter, and the heights of 3D polylines become ground levels. Build Network from Lines Layer > Build Network from Lines (or right-click a line layer, Build Network from This Layer) makes a new network layer from line layers already in the project. Tick the layers to use (each is highlighted on the map as you choose), and for each one the fields that hold the diameter, roughness, material, name and ground level, with a value to use where a field is empty. Set the snapping tolerance that joins line ends that nearly meet, whether lines are split where another ends on them (tees), and whether a junction is put where two lines cross (untick it when pipes cross at different depths without being connected), and whether pipes that meet end to end with the same properties are joined. Preview counts the pipes, junctions and joins it will make; Generate adds the network as a layer of its own, ready to run. Dropping line files on the Networks group in the Layers panel does the same. Check and Fix Network Layer > Check and Fix Network (the second page of the Network Builder) finds what a drawing or an import leaves wrong in a network layer, within a tolerance in metres: pipes that cross with no junction, and pipe ends that lie on another pipe with no junction; ends that run just past the pipe they should join (overshoots) or stop just short of it (undershoots); junctions closer together than the tolerance, pipes drawn twice, pipes with no length and junctions with no pipe; parts of the network with no reservoir or tank (reported for you to decide). Check lists them; click a row to select the elements and zoom to the place. Fix Ticked fixes the ticked ones together: junctions are put where pipes cross or meet, overshooting tails are cut off, short ends are joined to the pipe, doubled pipes and loose junctions are removed, and levels of new junctions are taken along their pipe. The whole fix is one step that Undo puts back.

Vector layers hold points, lines and polygons that are not a network: plots and parcels, roads, rivers, service areas, valve chambers, survey lines. New Shapefile Layer (Layer menu, or the first button of the Digitizing toolbar) creates a layer of points, multipoints, lines, multilines, polygons or multipolygons, as a new shapefile is created in a GIS: give it a name, its geometry type, its coordinate system and its fields (text, whole number, decimal number, date or yes/no). A new layer starts with an id field that numbers each new feature by itself (1, 2, 3) and a name field; with Number new features automatically ticked, adding a point does not stop to ask for its values: fill them in later in the attribute table. The layer is written as a shapefile where you choose, or kept in the project only. Layer > Add Vector Layer reads shapefiles, GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KML and DXF files as editable layers (not as a network): a file with several layers, or with points, lines and polygons together, gives one vector layer for each. Vector layers are listed under Vector layers and saved with the project (the layers read from one file, such as the drawing layers of a DXF or the tables of a GeoPackage, sit under a group named after the file, which shows or hides them together); right-click one to reproject it to another coordinate system. DXF drawings as vector layers A DXF added as a vector layer asks which of its drawing layers to bring in, and comes in as the drawing is organised: one vector layer for each drawing layer and kind of geometry (points, lines, polygons), or one for each kind when the drawing layers are not split. Blocks are drawn where they are inserted, texts become a labelled point layer at their height and angle, and every feature keeps its drawing layer, line type, colour and handle, with the colour of the drawing on the map. 3D entities keep their elevation in a field, so contour lines of a survey keep their level and can make a DEM. A DXF does not say its coordinate system: choose the one its coordinates are in. Selecting features The Select Features button (on the Selection toolbar, and in Vector > Selection) selects the features of any vector layer, whether it is being edited or not. A click on it selects in the way last chosen; the arrow beside it opens every way to select: Select by Click or Box: click a feature, or drag a box over several. Select by Drawn Polygon: click the corners of a polygon; a double-click, Enter or a right-click selects what it touches. With either, Shift adds to the selection, Ctrl takes from it (Ctrl and a click on a feature that is not selected adds it), and Esc clears the selection. Select by Expression (area_ha > 2 and crop == 'maize'), Select by Spatial Relation (the features that intersect, lie within, contain, touch, cross, overlap, are apart from or are near the features of another layer, or only its selected ones), Select All, Invert Selection and Clear Selection. There is one selection tool f...

section: Georeferencing and tracing a map or drawing
text: Layer > Georeferencer places a scanned map, a drawing, a photo or a page of a PDF on the map. A PDF asks for its page first: every page is shown as a preview with its sheet size (A1 landscape, for example), and the chosen page is drawn on white at 150 to 400 dpi and kept as an image beside the PDF. There is one Georeferencer window: it opens empty, or with the image chosen in the Layers panel, and Add Image loads another. Opening another image (or the practice map) asks first whether to save the point pairs of the one shown. Add Point: click points on the image (grid crossings, road junctions, building corners). Each click adds a row to the table; the window stays where it is, so you can add all the image points first. Select a row and click Pick Map Point: the main map comes forward, click the same place on it (or type its coordinates in the table), and the window comes back with the next row waiting. Pick on Map Only works on the main map alone: click a point of the overlaid image, then where it belongs, pair after pair; the window returns when the chosen method has the pairs it needs. The table shows each pair with its residual and the fit its RMS error. Delete Point (or the Delete key) removes the selected pair. Undo and Redo (Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Y) step back and forward through the pairs and the placement; Place in View puts the whole image in the middle of the map as a starting position, and Reset Placement returns it to where it was when opened. The second row of buttons keeps the result: Load Points, Save Points, Save World File and Export GeoTIFF (a georeferenced copy of the image, added as a layer). When it fits, Trace Over Image keeps the image faintly under the network and starts the pipe tool, so the network is drawn along the lines of the image. The image's Layer Properties have a Georeferencing page with its state. To learn it, open File > Open Sample Projects > Georeferencing practice map (or the Practice Map button): a scanned-style sheet with a coordinate grid in UTM zone 36 South. Load Points with practice_map.points beside it for nine pairs at grid crossings, or add your own by typing the grid coordinates written on the sheet.

Layer > Basemaps and Satellite Imagery (or the satellite button) adds online maps under the network: Group Basemaps Satellite imagery Esri World Imagery, Esri Clarity, Esri Firefly, Google Satellite, Google Satellite Hybrid, Bing Virtual Earth Street maps OpenStreetMap, Esri World Street Map, Carto Positron, Dark Matter and Voyager, Google Maps Topographic and terrain Google Terrain, Google Terrain Hybrid, OpenTopoMap, Esri World Topographic, Hillshade, National Geographic Vector basemaps ESRI Colored Pencil, Dark, Modern Antique, Nova, Night, Topo, Charted Territory, OSM Standard, OSM Street, OSM Light Grey, OSM Dark Grey, OSM Blueprint Labels and overlays place names, boundaries and roads to put over imagery Vector basemaps are drawn from map data with their own style (patterns, line styles and labels), so they stay sharp at every zoom. Tiles are kept on disk, so maps already seen also work offline. Respect each provider's terms of use; any other service can be added as a custom tile address with {z}, {x} and {y} (or {q} for quadkey services). Once a day FlowCHAOS checks in the background that every catalogue service still answers; one that has been retired is greyed out in the menus.

The Measure button measures distances, areas and perimeters, and angles and bearings. The Measure panel, under Element Properties, shows the values without covering the map, with the units to use: metres, kilometres, feet, yards, miles, nautical miles, centimetres, millimetres, inches, degrees or map units for lengths; square metres, square kilometres, hectares, acres, square feet, yards, miles, nautical miles, centimetres, millimetres, inches, square degrees or map units for areas; degrees, radians, gradians, mils or degrees, minutes and seconds for angles. Its buttons start again, copy the values and close (clearing the drawing and returning to Select); Esc clears it too. The default units of the project are set in Project Properties > Measurements, with Measure areas: on the ellipsoid (the default, as the areas of vector features) or on the map grid.

Layer > Merge Network Layers (or right-click a network layer > Merge Other Networks Into This) joins other network layers into one. Nodes closer than the join distance become one node; a node of one network lying on a pipe of the other splits that pipe and connects there; ends within the connection distance can be joined by a new pipe. Pipes, pumps and valves that are the same in both are kept once. The report lists what was joined, connected and left apart.

The project has one coordinate system (status bar, or Project Properties > Coordinates). A file opened into an empty project keeps its own system: the project takes it, and nothing is reprojected until you choose another system yourself. A network added to a project in another system is transformed into the project's system, and its original system is kept with the layer. When you import points, choose the system they were surveyed in. Vector and raster layers in other systems are drawn in the project's system as they are. Right-click a vector layer > Reproject Layer to add a copy in another system (save it with Save As), or a raster layer > Save Reprojected Copy. Properties > Coordinate system of a vector layer only changes the system it is read in, for a file that was labelled wrongly.

Double-click a layer (or use the properties button above the list): Symbology: for points (junctions, tanks, reservoirs) the colour, size and opacity; for lines (pipes, pumps, valves) the colour, thickness and pattern (solid, dashed, dotted, dash and dot). A map view, when one is chosen, colours the layer instead. Labels: see Map views, legends and labels. Fields: every field with its type, how many features fill it and an example value. Display: show the layer only between two map scales. Metadata: author and abstract, saved with the project. Project Properties > Data Sources lists every file the project uses; missing rasters can be pointed at their new location there.
New and moved nodes take their ground level automatically. Choose the source in Project Properties > Elevation: a DEM, online terrain, or none (type levels by hand).

Find and Query (Edit menu, Ctrl+F, or the toolbar) is a tool window beside the map, for network elements and vector features alike. Find matches names as you type, in all elements, one type (junctions, reservoirs, tanks, pipes, pumps, valves) or one vector layer (any text value of its features), by contains, starts with, exact or ends with, optionally with the links of the nodes found. When the project has several network layers, choose the one to search in, or all of them. Query runs on the layer you choose, named in full: the nodes or links of one network layer, of all network layers, or a vector layer. A query is made of conditions (a field, a comparison and a value) that must all hold, or any of them, or of an expression such as pressure_m < 10 and node_type == 'JUNCTION' built with the Expression Builder. The comparisons are below, at most, equal to, not equal to, at least, above, between (10 and 20), one of (110, 160, 200 or PVC, HDPE), contains, does not contain, starts with, ends with, is empty and is not empty. Invert finds the ones that do not match. New Query starts again; double-click a condition to change it, and Delete removes it. The label above the matches says exactly what was run and on which layer, and with several networks each match shows the network it belongs to. Save Query keeps a query by name with the project. Each saved query runs on its own, on its own layer, with Run (or a double-click); Load into the Editor brings it back to change, and saved queries can be renamed and removed. The matches are listed with the value that matched. Select on Map makes them a new selection, adds them to it, takes them from it or keeps only those already selected; Zoom To, Copy IDs and Export CSV act on the selected rows, or on all of them.

Attribute Table opens the table of the layer selected in the Layers panel: each imported network layer has its own table, and an open table is brought forward rather than opened twice. Selection is shared with the map both ways: selecting rows selects those elements on the map, and selecting on the map highlights their rows. Edits in the table can be undone like any other edit.
Label any layer by any field: one value, several values with units, or your own expression.

Every network layer is labelled in its Layer Properties > Labels tab, its nodes and its pipes apart. A layer without labels of its own follows Map Options > Labels, which sets the labels of the whole project; new projects show the IDs of nodes and pipes. The label switches and the right-click menu change the same settings, so they always agree.

Mode Example One field 110 (the diameter) Several fields with units P12 D=110 mm v=1.20 m/s Expression {name} D={diameter_mm} mm Fields include everything an element has: its name and type, levels, withdrawal, diameter, length, roughness and material, every column of the file it came from, and its results after a run.

Font, size, bold and italic, colour, a buffer (halo) and a background box, placement around points, offset, the scales between which labels show, priority and whether labels may overlap. A live example shows the first feature's label as you change the settings.
Only label where limits labels to the features that meet a condition, for example diameter_mm > 150 or name starts with PS.

Right-click a feature: Label Layer By labels its whole layer by one field in one step; Layer Labels... opens the full settings; Label changes only this feature: hide or show its label, give it its own text, move it, or change its size and colour. Reset to the Layer's Labels undoes that.
The elements of a network, the data each one carries, and the physics FlowCHAOS applies to them.

Junctions A junction is a point where pipes meet and where water can be taken out (or put in, as a negative withdrawal). Its data: Property Meaning Ground elevation the level of the ground at the junction, from a DEM, online terrain or typed in Design offset how far the pipe lies below (negative) or above the ground; the hydraulic elevation is ground plus offset Design withdrawal the average flow taken at the junction (L/s), the base demand Demand profile multipliers of the withdrawal through the day; none means the project's default profile Demand categories several withdrawals at one junction, each with its own profile (houses, a school, a leak), as imported models give them; FlowCHAOS keeps and analyses them Outflow coefficient an emitter: an outflow that grows with pressure, q = C p^n, for leaks, sprinklers and hydrants Starting concentration the water quality at the start of a run Injection a water quality source here (see Water quality) The analysis gives each junction its head, its pressure (head minus hydraulic elevation), the withdrawal actually delivered, and its water quality. Reservoirs A reservoir is a source or sink of unlimited capacity whose water level does not change with the flow: a lake, a river, a groundwater aquifer at its pumping level, or a connection to a bulk supply. Property Meaning Total head the level of the water surface (m above datum) Water level above ground another way to set it: the head follows the ground level when it changes Head profile multipliers that make the level vary in time (a tide, a river that rises and falls) Starting concentration, injection the quality of the water it supplies A borehole is modelled as a reservoir at its pumping water level (static level plus drawdown), with the submersible pump as a pump link from it. Tanks A tank stores water; its level rises when more flows in than out and falls otherwise. Property Meaning Ground elevation and stand height the bottom of the tank is the ground plus the stand (for an elevated tank) Diameter of a cylindrical tank Minimum, maximum and starting levels the water depth limits and the depth at the start of the run Minimum volume water below the minimum level that is never used Shape curve volume against depth for tanks that are not cylinders; the diameter is then ignored Spills when full extra inflow is lost over the top, rather than the inlet being closed Mixing behaviour, inlet zone fraction, decay rate in tank how water mixes and reacts inside it (see Water quality) When a tank reaches its maximum level its inflow stops (unless it spills); when it reaches its minimum level its outflow stops. Pipes A pipe carries water from its start node to its end node; the flow is negative when water runs the other way. Property Meaning Length taken from the drawing, or a model length when the drawing is schematic Diameter internal diameter in mm Roughness the friction coefficient of the chosen head loss formula Fittings loss factor K the minor losses of bends, t...

section: Data that describe time and behaviour
text: Demand profiles multiply the design withdrawals, period by period (usually hourly over a day). The profile library has typical shapes to start from. Curves: pump head and efficiency against flow, tank volume against depth, head loss against flow for general purpose valves. The library has samples for each type. In an element's properties each curve field lists only the curves of its kind (a tank's Volume curve, a pump's Head-flow curve and Efficiency curve); the button beside it opens the library at that curve, or starts a new one of the right kind, and assigns it when you close the library. A pump's Speed profile and Tariff profile are chosen from the demand profiles. Controls change one pump, pipe or valve at a time or when a level or pressure crosses a value; rules combine several conditions (Controls and rules). Analysis options set the units, the friction formula, the demand model, the solver's limits and the times of an extended period (Analysis options).

For each moment the analysis solves two sets of equations together: conservation of mass at every junction: the flows in equal the flows out plus the withdrawal; conservation of energy along every link: the difference of head between its ends equals the head lost in a pipe or valve, or minus the head added by a pump. Friction Head lost to friction along a pipe of length L (m), diameter D (m) and flow Q (m3/s): Formula Head loss Roughness Use it for Hazen-Williams h = 10.67 L Q^1.852 / (C^1.852 D^4.87) C, larger is smoother water supply in the usual range of velocities Darcy-Weisbach h = f L V^2 / (2 g D) roughness height e (mm); f from the Colebrook-White law or the laminar law any fluid and flow, the most exact Chezy-Manning h = 10.29 n^2 L Q^2 / D^5.33 Manning n, smaller is smoother larger mains and open-channel habits Typical roughness of new pipe: Material Hazen-Williams C Darcy-Weisbach e (mm) Manning n PVC, HDPE, PE, PPR 145 to 150 0.0015 to 0.007 0.009 GRP 150 0.01 0.009 Copper 140 0.0015 0.010 Ductile iron, cement lined 130 to 140 0.03 to 0.1 0.011 to 0.012 Steel, cement lined 130 to 140 0.05 0.012 Galvanised iron 120 0.15 0.014 Concrete 120 to 140 0.3 to 3 0.012 to 0.015 Old cast iron 60 to 100 1 to 5 0.015 to 0.017 Roughness grows as pipes age and scale; calibrate it against field pressures and flows. Minor losses Fittings add a loss h = K V^2 / (2 g), with K the sum of the loss factors of the bends, tees, valves and meters along the pipe (a gate valve fully open about 0.2, a 90 degree bend about 0.3 to 0.9, a globe valve about 10). Pumps A pump adds the head of its curve at the flow through it. A curve given by one point (the design flow and head) is extended to a full curve with shut-off at 133 % of the design head and the largest flow at twice the design flow. A three-point curve (shut-off, design, largest flow) is fitted by a smooth law; a curve with more points is followed point by point. At a relative speed s the curve scales as h(sQ) = s^2 h(Q). Demand-driven and pressure-driven withdrawal In a demand-driven analysis every junction receives its full withdrawal whatever the pressure; negative pressures then show where the network cannot deliver it. In a pressure-driven analysis the delivered withdrawal follows the pressure p: nothing below the minimum pressure Pmin; the full withdrawal Q at or above the required pressure Preq; in between, q = Q ((p - Pmin) / (Preq - Pmin))^n, usually with n = 0.5. Pressure-driven analysis is the one to use for intermittent supply, for networks that cannot meet the peak, and for any study of what customers actually receive. Emitters An outflow coefficient C at a junction adds an outflow q = C p^n (n is the emitter exponent of the analysis options, 0.5 for an orifice). Emitters model leaks, sprinklers, fire hydrants and open taps.

The quality analysis follows the substance with the water. Its steps, at each quality time step: Transport: water moves along each pipe at its velocity, carrying its concentration in segments. Mixing at junctions: the water leaving a junction has the flow-weighted average of the water arriving, plus any source there. Mixing in tanks: by the tank's mixing behaviour: Behaviour How the tank mixes Typical tank Fully mixed all water in the tank mixes at once a tank with one pipe for inlet and outlet Two compartments an inlet zone mixes with the inflow, the rest only with the inlet zone a large tank with separate inlet and outlet Plug flow, first in first out water leaves in the order it came a tall tank with inlet and outlet at opposite ends Stacked, last in first out new water floats on old and leaves first a tank filled and emptied from the bottom Reactions: in the bulk water, at a rate kb C^n (first order, n = 1: the concentration falls exponentially, halving every ln 2 / kb days); at the pipe wall, at a rate that depends on the wall coefficient kw, the pipe size and how fast the substance can reach the wall (molecular diffusivity); a limiting potential makes a reaction stop at a level (a substance that grows to a ceiling or decays to a floor). Water age is computed as a substance that grows by one hour every hour; source tracing as the share of water that has passed through the traced node. Rates by material, bottle tests and the study tools are in Water quality.
Steady-state and extended-period analysis, demand models, controls and water quality.
Run Steady State (F5) solves the network for one moment with the advanced solver. Nodes without pipes, such as survey points, are left out automatically and counted in the status bar.

A project can hold its own network and networks imported as layers. They are separate systems, so an analysis works on one of them: the one whose layer is selected in the Layers panel, or the one chosen with Analysis > Network to Analyse. Steady-state and extended-period runs, pipe sizing, fire flow, criticality and the solver comparison all use that network, and the status bar names it. The run commands are available while a network layer is selected; if that network is out of view, the map zooms to it when the run starts. In the Layers panel, the third column marks the network that has results (a ticked sheet) and the one being analysed (a turning sign); the Simulation Results title names it too.

FlowCHAOS can solve a model without opening its window, for batch studies and scripts: FlowCHAOS --run model.inp report.txt --hours 24 --step-minutes 60 The model may be any network file or project FlowCHAOS opens. Without a report name the full report is printed in the console; without --hours the run is a steady state.

Run Extended Period follows the network through time with demand profiles, tank levels, pump schedules and controls. Enter the duration and the time step. The run happens in the background; the window stays usable and the results arrive when it finishes. While it runs, the status bar shows the elapsed time, the simulated time reached and a progress bar that fills step by step; the run time is given when it ends. Use the time bar to step through the results or play them; the map, tables, legends and animations follow the time shown. The Simulation Results panel opens by itself the first time results arrive.

Stop / Clear Results stops a running analysis (its results are ignored when they arrive) or, when nothing is running, clears the results so the map shows the network as drawn. Undo brings the results back.

After every run the solver's warnings are kept with the results: a system that did not balance or may be unstable, negative pressures, disconnected nodes, pumps running outside their curve and valves that cannot hold their setting. The completion message says how many there are; Analysis > Solver Warnings lists them, and a double-click selects the pump, valve or node named.

Settings > Hydraulic Solver chooses the algorithm for steady-state runs: Algorithm Unknowns Character Advanced engine (recommended) flows and heads Global gradient with every valve, pump, control, rule and water-quality option Built-in sparse Newton flows and heads Newton with least-squares safeguards; pressure-driven withdrawal and control valves Global gradient (Todini and Pilati, 1988) flows and heads Newton reduced to a symmetric system in the heads; continuity holds after each iteration Newton nodal (Martin and Peters, 1963) heads Newton on the junction heads alone, damped by a line search Linear theory (Wood and Charles, 1972) flows and heads Linearised elements solved exactly, flows averaged between iterations Hardy Cross (1936) loop flows One loop corrected at a time, with pseudo-loops between sources The four comparison algorithms solve the same equations with the same head loss formula, minor losses, pump curves (one-point and three-point curves are fitted as the standard method does) and emitters. Pressure and flow control valves, controls and rules are modelled by the advanced engine and the built-in solver; extended-period runs always use the advanced engine.

Analysis Options > Hydraulics > Demand chooses the demand model. Demand-driven (DDA) delivers every withdrawal whatever the pressure. Pressure-driven (PDA) delivers what the pressure allows: nothing below the minimum pressure, the full withdrawal at the required pressure, and in between q = Q ((p - Pmin) / (Preq - Pmin))^n, with n = 0.5 for orifices such as hydrants and sprinklers. PDA works in every analysis: steady and extended-period runs, pipe sizing, fire flow, criticality, water quality and the solver comparison. The global gradient, Newton nodal and linear theory algorithms solve it as well as the engine; Hardy Cross balances loops around fixed withdrawals and says so. Set the required pressure from what the outlet serves: an open canal needs little, a hose or a sprinkler much more.

Analysis > Compare Solvers runs the network with the algorithms you tick and lists, for each: whether it converged, iterations, time, the largest continuity and energy errors, and the largest and RMS differences in head and flow from a reference algorithm, with the node and link where they occur. A chart shows the convergence history on a logarithmic scale, and the window recommends an algorithm for the network. Use for Runs makes the selected algorithm the one steady-state runs use; Export CSV saves the table and every iteration for a report or a paper.

Analysis > Analysis Options has a tab for each subject: Hydraulics (units, head loss formula, demand model, pressure-driven settings, convergence), Water Quality, Reactions, Times, Energy, and the ID Labels and Element Defaults of new elements (see Drawing).

Scheduled Pipe Controls: a pump, pipe or valve opened, closed, slowed or reset at a time, at a time of day, or when a tank level or a junction pressure crosses a value. Rule-Based Controls: IF / AND / OR / THEN / ELSE rules on pressures, levels, flows, demand and time, with priorities. Both start from samples written with the network's own elements; see Controls and rules. Demand Profiles and the Performance Curve Library for profiles, pump and valve curves. The curve library starts a curve of any kind from a sample (borehole, solar, surface, booster and transfer pumps; efficiency curves; horizontal, spherical and conical tanks; strainers, meters, filters and backflow preventers), and Delete Curves lists every curve with what uses it. The profile editor has presets from the literature to start from: urban, suburban, weekend, peri-urban and rural water points, intermittent supply, offices, schools, hospitals, hotels, industry in one or two shifts or continuous, irrigation by day, by night, in two sets or in drip pulses, livestock, night-time leakage, and monthly and weekly profiles. Each is scaled to an average of 1.0 and shows where its shape comes from; edit the values to measured use.

Analysis > Water Quality Analysis follows chlorine, a chemical, the age of the water or the share of water from one source, with ready studies for chlorine compliance, boosters, water age, source tracing and contamination events, compliance by delivered water and a PDF report. See Water quality.

The node table lists head, pressure, delivered withdrawal and quality; the link table lists start and end nodes, diameter, length, flow, velocity, velocity head, heads, total energy, head loss and residual head. Choose the columns with Columns, filter by name, and sort by any column. Select cells (or whole rows and columns) and right-click to Copy or Copy with Headers: the cells paste as a table into spreadsheets, documents and text editors. Ctrl+C works too, in every table of the program. Analysis > Export Results writes a spreadsheet with a sheet for nodes and one for links.

Every option of Analysis > Analysis Options: what it does, its usual value and when to change it. Analysis > Analysis Options has a tab for each subject. The options are kept with the project and written into the hydraulic model file when the network is exported. Point at any field for a short explanation.

Units and friction Option Choices or range Default Meaning Flow units L/s, L/min, ML/day, m3/hour, m3/day, US gal/min, ft3/s, US Mgal/day, Imperial Mgal/day, acre-ft/day L/s units of flow in the project and its exchange files; metric flow units keep the other quantities metric Head loss formula Hazen-Williams, Darcy-Weisbach, Chezy-Manning Hazen-Williams the friction law; each pipe keeps a roughness for each formula, so switching back and forth loses nothing Specific gravity 0.01 to 100 1.0 density of the fluid relative to water at 4 degrees C Relative viscosity 0.001 to 1000 1.0 kinematic viscosity relative to water at 20 degrees C; used by Darcy-Weisbach Demand Option Default Meaning Demand model Demand-driven Demand-driven delivers every withdrawal whatever the pressure; pressure-driven delivers what the pressure allows Demand multiplier 1.0 scales every withdrawal of the run: 1.8 for a peak hour, 0.4 for night flow Default demand profile 1 the profile of withdrawals that name none Emitter exponent 0.5 the exponent n of emitter outflow q = C p^n (0.5 for orifices, sprinklers and most leaks; 0.5 to 1.5 for leaks in plastic pipe) Pressure-driven withdrawal Used when the demand model is pressure-driven. Option Default Meaning Minimum pressure 0 m at or below this pressure nothing is delivered Required pressure 0.1 m at or above this pressure the full withdrawal is delivered; set it from what the outlet serves (a yard tap 5 to 10 m, a house connection 15 to 20 m, a sprinkler 25 to 35 m) Pressure exponent 0.5 the shape of the delivery curve between the two pressures Convergence Option Default Meaning Maximum trials 40 iterations allowed for one hydraulic state Accuracy 0.001 the state has converged when the sum of the flow changes, divided by the total flow, is below this Maximum head error 0 (not checked) largest error allowed in the head loss of any link, in metres Maximum flow change 0 (not checked) largest flow change allowed in any link at convergence Status check frequency 2 iterations between checks of pump, valve and check valve status Status checks up to trial 10 after this trial, status is checked only at convergence Damping limit 0 (none) below this accuracy, flow corrections are halved to settle hard networks If a state does not converge Stop the run stop the extended period, or continue with a warning Status report Changes of status what the solver reports: status changes, nothing, or every trial (for diagnosing a network that will not balance) Raise Maximum trials to 200 for large or difficult networks. A network that does not converge is usually a modelling problem (a closed loop of valves, a pump that cannot lift, disconnected nodes): Analysis > Solver Warnings names the elements involved.

Option Default Meaning Parameter None what extended-period runs follow: chlorine, a chemical, water age or source tracing Traced source the node whose water is traced Quality tolerance 0.01 the smallest difference of quality that keeps two parcels of water apart Relative diffusivity 1 molecular diffusivity relative to chlorine in water; 0 means wall reactions are not limited by mass transfer For a full study use Analysis > Water Quality Analysis (Water quality).

Option Default Meaning Bulk reaction order 1 order of the reaction in the water Wall reaction order 1 0 or 1 Tank reaction order 1 order of the reaction in tanks Global bulk coefficient 0 bulk rate of every pipe without its own (1/day, negative for decay) Global wall coefficient 0 wall rate of every pipe without its own (m/day for first order) Limiting potential 0 (none) a concentration a reaction tends to and stops at Roughness correlation 0 (none) makes wall rates follow pipe roughness, so older pipes react more

Durations and steps are written as H:MM or H:MM:SS. Option Default Meaning Simulation duration 0:00 the length of an extended period (0 is a steady state) Hydraulic timestep 1:00 the step between hydraulic solutions; shorter steps follow tanks and controls more closely Quality timestep 0:05 the step of the quality transport; shorter is more accurate Profile timestep 1:00 the length of one period of the demand profiles Profile start 0:00 the period of the profiles at the start of the run Report timestep 1:00 how often results are kept Report start 0:00 the time from which results are kept Rule timestep 0:00:10 how often rules are checked between hydraulic steps Start clock time 12 am the time of day when the run starts; clock-time controls and rules count from it

Option Default Meaning Global pump efficiency 75 % the efficiency of pumps without an efficiency curve Global energy price 0 price of a kWh for pumps without their own tariff Energy price profile multipliers of the price through the day (a night tariff); a pump can have its own in its properties Demand charge 0 a charge per kW of the highest pumping power Analysis > Energy Report gives, for each pump, the share of the time it runs, its mean flow, head and efficiency, the energy per cubic metre pumped, its mean and peak power, and its energy and cost per day, with the totals, the peak power of all pumps together and the demand charge. In an extended period the energy is summed over every time step, with the efficiency at each step's flow (from the pump's efficiency curve) and the price at that time of day.

ID Labels sets the prefix, the first number and the step of the names of new elements (J1, J2; P1, P2 and so on). Element Defaults gives new junctions their design offset and withdrawal, new tanks their size and levels, and new pipes and valves their diameter, roughness and material, so a network can be drawn quickly and corrected afterwards.

Switch pumps, pipes and valves during a run: simple controls, rules, and ready-made samples. Controls change a pump, a pipe or a valve while an extended-period run goes on: a pump that fills a tank and stops when it is full, a main closed for a repair, a valve that lowers night pressure. FlowCHAOS has two kinds. Simple controls have one trigger and one action each. Rules combine several conditions with AND and OR, have an ELSE, and a priority that settles conflicts. Both editors offer samples written with your network's own pumps, tanks, valves and pipes, so a sample runs as soon as it is added and you only change the numbers.

Analysis > Scheduled Pipe Controls lists one control per row: Column Meaning Link The pump, pipe or valve the control changes Set to OPEN, CLOSED, or a number: the relative speed of a pump (1.0 is full speed) or the setting of a valve (pressure in m for a pressure valve, flow for a flow valve) Trigger At elapsed time, At clock time, When node rises above, When node falls below Time For a time trigger: hours into the run (6 or 6:30); for a clock time: 6 AM, 10:30 PM or 22:00 Node and Level or pressure For a level trigger: a tank (its water level above its bottom) or a junction (its pressure), and the value in metres The box under the table reads the selected control as a sentence, for example "Open PU1 every day at 10 PM. Runs in the advanced engine.", and turns red with the reason when a control cannot run (a pipe given a speed, a node that is not in the network, a time with 75 minutes). The row number shows the same warning. OK refuses a control that cannot run and says why. Start from a sample offers, depending on what the network has: Fill the tank: pump on when low, off when full: the pump starts below a low level and stops above a high level, taken from the tank's own minimum and maximum levels. Night-time pumping on the cheap tariff: the pump runs from 10 PM to 6 AM. Slower pump in the day, full speed at night: 80 % speed from 6 AM, full speed from 10 PM. Pipe shut for a repair from hour 8 to hour 12: who loses water during a repair. Open a bypass when pressure drops: a pipe opens below 15 m at the highest junction and closes again above 25 m. Lower the valve setting at night: less pressure, and less leakage, from 11 PM to 5 AM. Close the tank inlet before it overflows. Imported controls in other forms, or naming an element that is no longer in the network, are kept unchanged and listed under the table. Elapsed-time controls that open or close run in every solver; clock times, speeds, settings and level or pressure triggers run in the advanced engine, which is the default for extended-period runs.

Analysis > Rule-Based Controls edits the rules as text, one clause a line: RULE PumpOn IF TANK T1 LEVEL BELOW 1.5 THEN PUMP PU1 STATUS IS OPEN PRIORITY 2 Clause Form RULE RULE and a name, one word IF object id attribute relation value AND, OR more conditions (AND also adds actions after THEN) THEN PUMP, PIPE, VALVE or LINK id STATUS or SETTING IS value ELSE the action when the conditions are false PRIORITY a number; when two rules disagree, the higher priority wins Objects: JUNCTION, TANK, RESERVOIR, NODE, PIPE, PUMP, VALVE, LINK and SYSTEM. Node attributes: PRESSURE, HEAD, LEVEL, DEMAND, FILLTIME and DRAINTIME (hours to fill or drain a tank). Link attributes: FLOW, STATUS, SETTING and POWER. System: TIME (hours into the run), CLOCKTIME (10 PM, 06:00) and DEMAND (total demand). Relations: =, <>, <, >, <=, >=, IS, NOT, ABOVE and BELOW. A semicolon starts a comment. The editor colours keywords, objects, attributes, relations and numbers. The samples on the left, for this network: Pump follows the tank level: two rules keep the tank between a low and a high level. Night tariff with a full-tank guard: the pump fills the tank at night while it has room, and rests in the day unless the tank is nearly empty; an emergency rule with a higher priority starts it whenever the level is very low. Pump speed follows the town's demand: full speed above 120 % of the average demand, 75 % otherwise, as a variable speed drive does. Duty and standby pumps: the second pump starts only when the first cannot keep up. Pressure management at the critical point: a pressure valve raises its setting when the highest junction falls below 15 m. Burst drill: isolate a main for four hours. Tank overflow protection: the inlet shuts when the tank is nearly full, with the highest priority. Fire reserve: the pump starts when the level is low or the tank would drain within two hours. Add to Rules appends the selected sample (a double-click does the same; rules that would share a name are renamed), Replace Rules starts again from the sample alone. Check reads every clause against the network: unknown keywords, objects and attributes, names that are not in the network, a pump called a pipe, a pipe given a setting, a rule without a THEN, two rules with the same name. Each problem is listed with its line; click it to go to the line. OK checks too and asks before keeping rules with problems. Rules run in the advanced engine.

Give a pump that a rule controls a starting status in its properties; rules change it from the first time step on. Use a gap between the start and stop levels of a tank (at least half a metre) so the pump does not start and stop at every step. Watch the result with Show on Map and the time bar, or plot the tank level and the pump flow under Analysis > Advanced Graphs.

Chlorine residuals, water age, source tracing and contamination events, from set-up to a report. Analysis > Water Quality Analysis follows a substance or the age of the water through an extended-period run of the network. It is built for the questions a water utility answers every day: does every customer receive enough free chlorine, where does the water stay too long, which works feeds which zone, and what happens if something enters the network. The window has the study set-up on the left, in the order you fill it, and the results on the right. Everything you set is kept with the project, so the next time the window opens the same study is ready to run again.

The first box offers ready studies. Each one fills every part of the set-up with this network's own reservoirs, tanks and nodes, so it runs at once and you only change the numbers. Study What it answers Main settings Chlorine residual compliance Does every junction keep enough free chlorine? Chlorine 1 mg/L leaving each reservoir, bulk decay -0.55 per day, wall decay by pipe material, limits 0.2 to 5 mg/L, 72 h with 24 h of warm-up Chlorine with a booster at the service tanks Does re-dosing at the tanks keep the far end above 0.2 mg/L? As above, plus a 0.6 mg/L set-point at every tank Water age and tank turnover Where is the water older than 72 hours? Water age over 168 h, statistics from hour 96 Where each source's water goes Which zone does each works serve, and where do sources blend? Source tracing from the first reservoir Contamination event Which nodes does a contaminant reach, when, and how strongly? A mass injection at a central junction from hour 2 to hour 4, 48 h at 15 minute steps, reached above 0.01 mg/L Fluoride or another conservative chemical Does any junction exceed a maximum? A chemical that does not decay, limit 1.5 mg/L Custom study keeps whatever you set below. Changing the parameter by hand switches back to a custom study and fills in the usual limits of the new parameter.

Parameter Unit Meaning Chlorine (free residual) mg/L A reacting substance: it decays in the water and at the pipe walls Water age h The time since the water left a source; tanks and dead ends age it Source tracing % The share of the water at each node that came from the traced source Chemical mg/L Any substance, conservative (no decay) or reacting For source tracing, choose the traced source: a reservoir, a tank or any node. The window lists reservoirs and tanks first.
