Each row is one source at one node: Type Strength means Use it for Inflow the concentration of water entering the network at a reservoir or tank (mg/L) treatment works, a borehole with its own dosing Set-point the concentration the node keeps in the water leaving it (mg/L) a booster chlorinator at a tank or a pumping station Flow-paced the concentration the node adds to the water passing through (mg/L) a dosing pump paced by a flow meter Mass the mass added each minute (mg/min) a spill, an intrusion, a tracer test From (h) and To (h) limit a source to part of the run: an accidental intrusion from hour 2 to hour 4, a booster switched on at hour 12, a dosing failure from hour 30. To at 0 means to the end of the run. The source is switched on and off on the time step of the demand profiles (one hour unless you changed it under Analysis Options, Times). Add adds an empty row, or one booster for every node selected on the map; Remove deletes the selected row. Sources only matter for chlorine and chemicals: water age and tracing need none.

Bulk: the first-order decay rate of the water itself, per day (negative for decay). Free chlorine usually lies between -0.1 and -1.5 per day; warm water and water rich in organic matter decay faster. From a bottle test: fill a dark bottle with water leaving the works, keep it at a steady temperature and read the chlorine twice. Enter the two readings, the hours between them, the bottle temperature and the usual temperature of the water in the network. FlowCHAOS works out the rate, corrects it to the network temperature (the rate changes by a factor of about 1.07 for every degree; you can change the factor) and shows how long chlorine takes to halve. Wall: the rate at which pipe walls consume chlorine, in m/day. One rate for every pipe uses the value below. By pipe material gives each pipe the rate of its material; Rates shows every material class, how many pipes of the network belong to it, and its rate: Material Typical wall rate (m/day) HDPE / PE, uPVC / PVC -0.01 GRP -0.02 Copper -0.05 Ductile iron (lined), asbestos cement, concrete -0.1 Steel -0.3 Galvanised iron -0.4 Cast iron (unlined) -0.5 These are starting values to calibrate with field readings. A pipe whose material is not recognised uses the single wall rate; a pipe with its own wall rate in its properties keeps it. Tank decay: the bulk rate inside tanks, the same as in pipes unless you untick As in pipes. Tank mixing: how the water mixes inside the tanks. Complete mixing suits a tank with one pipe for inlet and outlet; Two compartments splits the volume into a zone that mixes with the inflow (its share is the number beside it) and a zone that does not; Plug flow (first in, first out) suits a tall tank with separate inlet and outlet; Stacked (last in, first out) suits a tank where new water floats on old. As each tank is set keeps the model in each tank's properties. Initial value: the value everywhere at the start; tanks start full of it.

Minimum and Maximum: the range every junction must keep, for example free chlorine from 0.2 to 5 mg/L (WHO guidelines), water age at most 72 hours, fluoride at most 1.5 mg/L. Reached above: a junction counts as reached the first time its value rises above this level. The results then give the hour each junction is first reached: the arrival time of a contaminant, or of water from a new source.

Duration: long enough for tanks and remote pipes to settle; three days for chlorine, a week for water age. Warm-up: the first hours are left out of the statistics while values settle from their starting state. Results every and Quality step: how often results are kept, and the transport step (shorter is more accurate and slower). Run Water Quality Analysis solves the hydraulics and the transport together with the advanced engine. The window stays usable while it runs.

Summary opens with a coloured verdict: green when every junction stays within the limits, amber when a few leave them, red when many do or when a contaminant reaches junctions. Below it: the number of junctions, the mean, the lowest and the highest value; how many junctions stay within the limits at all times; water delivered within the limits: the share of the water actually delivered to customers (each junction's delivered demand over the time) that met the limits. A dead end that fails but serves few people weighs little; a busy zone that fails weighs a lot. This is the figure a board or a regulator asks for; the junctions that leave the limits, with the share of time they stay within them; for a contamination event, the junctions reached, the first to be reached and the arrival hour at each, and the water delivered at reached junctions; the tanks, and the study set-up, so a printed summary says how it was obtained. Nodes lists every node with its minimum, mean, maximum and final value, the share of time within the limits, the water delivered after the warm-up and the hour it was first reached. Sort by any column; double-click a row to find the node on the map. Tanks lists the tanks with their minimum, mean, maximum and final value. Time Series plots the selected nodes (up to six) over the run, with the limits as dashed lines and the end of the warm-up as a dotted line. Under the tabs: Show on Map puts the run on the map: Map Styles colours nodes and pipes by concentration, and the time bar and Animate Map play it. Select Failing Junctions selects on the map every junction that leaves the limits. Export CSV writes the node table and the full time series. Report (PDF) writes a printable report: the title, the network, the date, the verdict, the figures, the set-up and the junction table.

section: A worked example: chlorine in a town network
text: File > Open Sample Projects > Chlorine residual in a town network. Analysis > Water Quality Analysis. Choose Chlorine residual compliance. Click From a bottle test: first reading 1.0 mg/L, second reading 0.6 mg/L after 48 hours, bottle at 25 degrees, network at 22 degrees. The bulk rate becomes about -0.21 per day. Click OK. Run. The summary shows the lowest residual and where it occurs. Choose Chlorine with a booster at the service tanks and run again to see what re-dosing at the tanks changes. Report (PDF) for the file.

section: A worked example: a contamination event
text: Select the junction where the contaminant could enter, then choose Contamination event. In the sources table, set the node, the mass (mg/min) and the hours it lasts. Run. The verdict gives the number of junctions reached and the first arrival; the Nodes tab, sorted by First reached, gives the order in which to warn customers or close valves. Show on Map and play the time bar to watch the plume travel.

Run the hydraulics first (Run Extended Period) and fix any warnings: water quality follows the flows, so unbalanced hydraulics give meaningless concentrations. Use a warm-up of at least a day, longer when tanks are large compared with the demand. Calibrate the bulk rate with bottle tests, then the wall rates with chlorine readings at a few hydrants; the Field Observation Set (Analysis menu) holds the readings. The same settings drive every extended-period run when the parameter is set under Analysis Options > Water Quality; the Water Quality Analysis window adds the study tools on top.
Reading what an analysis found: the map, the tables, the graphs, the warnings and the reports.

After a run the results are kept with the project and appear in several places at once: the map: the Map Styles panel colours the nodes and links by any result, with a legend on the map (Map views, legends and animation); Element Properties: click a node or a link to read its values under Results; the Simulation Results panel: the time bar and the result tables; Analysis > Advanced Graphs: time series, profiles, contour plots, frequency plots and the system's flow balance; tool windows: pipe sizing, fire flow, criticality, water quality and the energy report each show their own results.

An extended period gives one set of results at every report step. The time bar at the top of the Simulation Results panel chooses the time shown; the map, tables, legends, labels and Element Properties all follow it. Play the run with the play button, step with the arrows, or choose a time from the list. Animate Map moves water along the pipes at the time shown, or through the run. Below the times, the list holds statistics over the run: the Minimum, Maximum, Average and Range of every result at every element. Choose one and the map, the tables and the legends show it, for example the lowest pressure each junction sees in the day.

Analysis > Status Report lists what happened during the run, in time order: pumps that started and stopped, valves that changed state, tanks that filled or emptied, controls and rules that acted, and warnings. For a water quality run it ends with the mass balance: what entered, left, reacted and is still stored, and the difference as a percentage. Analysis > Calibration Report compares the results with field measurements entered in Analysis > Field Observation Set (pressures, flows, levels or quality, at times you give): the mean and root mean square error at each location, the correlation of computed and measured values, and a chart of one against the other. Analysis > Full Report writes a text file with the options, every node and every link at every report time, for archives and checking by hand.

The Nodes table lists each node's head, pressure, delivered withdrawal and water quality; the Links table lists each link's start and end nodes, diameter, length, flow, velocity, velocity head, heads at both ends, head loss, friction gradient and status. Columns chooses the columns shown. Type in the filter box to show the rows whose name contains it. Click a column heading to sort by it; click again to reverse. Double-click a row to find the element on the map. Select cells, rows or columns and right-click to Copy or Copy with Headers; they paste as a table into spreadsheets and documents (Ctrl+C works too). Analysis > Export Results writes a spreadsheet with a sheet for the nodes and one for the links; for an extended period, the time chosen in the time bar.

Analysis > Advanced Graphs draws: Graph What it shows Use it to Time Series one value of one node or link through the run (pressure at a junction, level of a tank, flow of a pump) check that tanks fill and empty, pumps cycle sensibly and pressures stay up at peak Profile Plot a value along a path of nodes, from a start node to an end node see the hydraulic grade along a main, and where pressure is lost Contour Plot a value over the whole network, as coloured areas find the low-pressure zones at a glance Frequency Plot the share of nodes or links below each value state compliance: 95 % of junctions above 15 m System Flow the total production and consumption through the run check that supply meets demand and see the daily cycle Hover a point to read its value; the export button saves the graph as a PNG image at twice screen resolution. Edit > Longitudinal Profile draws the ground, the pipe invert, the cover and the hydraulic grade line along selected connected pipes, ready for a drawing sheet.

The solver reports what it noticed during the run: a time step that did not balance, negative pressures, disconnected nodes, pumps working outside their curve or unable to deliver the head, valves that cannot hold their setting, tanks that are full or empty. The completion message says how many there are; Analysis > Solver Warnings lists them with their times, and a double-click selects the element named. See Errors and warnings for what each one means and what to do.

A useful order for checking a design: Warnings first: a network that does not balance gives meaningless numbers. Pressures: every junction between the minimum (often 10 to 15 m for a public supply, 5 to 10 m at communal taps) and the maximum (often 60 to 80 m, to limit leakage and bursts), at the peak and at night. Velocities: typically 0.5 to 1.5 m/s in distribution and up to 2 to 2.5 m/s in short mains; very slow pipes keep water too long. Head loss: the friction gradient (m/km) shows undersized pipes; a few metres per kilometre is comfortable in a main. Tanks: levels that cycle within their range every day, neither emptying nor staying full. Pumps: running near their best efficiency, starting a few times a day rather than every hour. Water quality: chlorine above the minimum everywhere, water age below the limit. The limits come from the design standard of the project and the standards of your country or utility; FlowCHAOS shows the values, the engineer judges them.
Colour the network by any value, read it with legends, and bring the results to life.

The Map Styles panel (View > Map Styles, or its toolbar button) has a view for Nodes and one for Links, chosen independently. Views of the elements' own data, such as diameter or ground elevation, work at any time, before any run; result views become available after a run. Each list is grouped into Data and Results. A project opens with Layer colour, so each layer keeps its own colour until you choose a view. Nodes Links Data: ground level, hydraulic elevation, design withdrawal, starting concentration, pipe cover Data: diameter, model length, roughness, criticality, bulk and wall decay rates Results: pressure, hydraulic grade, delivered withdrawal, concentration, pressure above the minimum, withdrawal not delivered Results: velocity, flow, friction gradient (m/km), head loss, friction factor, decay reaction rate, concentration, travel time of the water, pressure class used (%), Reynolds number, velocity head Apply to at the top of the panel decides which layers take the view: the selected layer in the Layers panel, every network layer, or one layer you pick. The other layers keep their own colours, so two networks can be shown in different ways side by side. Colour the pipes by diameter to check a design at a glance, or the nodes by ground elevation to read the terrain under the network.

Each view has its own colour band, with the title above a full-width ramp; click it to choose a ramp, reverse it or split it into classes. The ramp list opens below the band, or above it when there is no room, and scrolls; every ramp chooser in FlowCHAOS works the same way. Nodes and links keep separate ramps, so changing one never changes the other. When the view's legend has classes, the band shows those classes and their break values. Double-click a class to change its colour, or choose Edit Classes and Colours in the ramp list to set the number of classes, the break values and every colour in the Legend Editor.

View > Map Options has a page for each part of the map: Nodes (which types are shown, size, opacity, shapes), Pipes and Links (pumps and valves shown, width, opacity, outline), Labels, Flow and Results (arrows and their size, sizing symbols by value), Selection (colour, halo and pulse) and Background and Drawing. Restore Defaults resets them. More settings on these pages: On the map: a scale bar and a north arrow, each in the corner you choose. View > Scale Bar and View > North Arrow switch them on and off quickly. Closed links dashed: closed pipes, stopped pumps and shut valves are drawn dashed, at the time shown. Hover information: resting the pointer on an element shows its name, type and main results. Design Checks: after a run the map marks what lies outside your limits, each check switched on by itself: pressure below the minimum, above the maximum, or negative; velocity below the minimum (water standing) or above the maximum; head loss per kilometre above the limit (the pipe is too small); pressure above the pipe's class (PN10 allows about 102 m); cover below the minimum where the pipe level was designed; pipes carrying almost nothing (water ageing); dead ends and nodes joined to nothing. A summary box in the corner you choose counts what each check found.

The legend button beside each band opens the Legend Editor: Continuous colours, equal intervals, equal counts (the same number of elements in each class) or your own break values; a colour per class (double-click a swatch) and a title. Legends are drawn on the map. Drag one to move it; click its small round x to hide it (the Legend Editor shows it again). Positions and classes are saved with the project, one legend per view. Colour relief and surface maps have their own colour band legend: right-click the layer and choose Show Legend on Map. Their icons in the Layers panel follow their colours, with a swatch for each class beneath them.

A legend in the top right corner of the map says what the moving marks mean: for the flow, the size of a mark at three flows and the fastest velocity; for the other animations, their colours and the values they stand for. It is drawn into saved videos and GIFs too; View > Animation > Show Animation Legend turns it off. Flow is shown as dots when FlowCHAOS starts; arrows and drops are in the same menu. Animate Map (run toolbar and results time bar) brings the map to life. The arrow beside it chooses what moves: Animation What you see Flow particles travelling along every pipe in its flow direction, faster where the water is faster; as dots, small arrows or water drops Head loss warm sparks along the pipes, denser and brighter where more energy is lost Water quality particles moving with the flow, coloured by the concentration Delivered withdrawal ripples spreading from the nodes, larger where more water is taken Pressure halos breathing around the nodes, in the colours of their pressure Design withdrawal ripples from the design withdrawal (no run needed) Roughness a texture drifting along the pipes, denser on rougher pipes (no run needed) During playback of an extended-period run the animation follows the time shown. Save Animation as Video or GIF (the arrow beside Animate Map, or the Analysis menu) saves the time steps of the results, the moving flow, or both together as an MP4 video or an animated GIF, at the speed, smoothness and size you choose, with the time written in a corner. Animate Map is available when there is something to animate: results of a run, or Design withdrawal or Roughness chosen in View > Animation (which works before any run).

Stop / Clear Results stops a running analysis, or clears the results so the map shows the network as drawn; Undo brings them back. A run itself is not an undo step (it is a calculation, not an edit of the network), so the results of earlier runs are not kept in memory; the undo history keeps the last 150 edits, so a long session never fills the memory.

Grid on the Drafting toolbar shows or hides the grid lines. Its arrow has Coordinate Labels and Rulers (bands along the top and left edges with a tick at every grid line), each on or off on its own, so the map can show lines only, labels or rulers only, or any mix (the grid lines alone at first); and Map Grid Settings. The grid is a preference of FlowCHAOS, the same in every project: changing it never leaves a project with unsaved changes. Spacing: automatic (round steps of 1, 2 and 5 that follow the zoom, a guide to the eye; points snap every 10 m) or a fixed spacing, which points snap to. Style: lines, dots at the crossings or small crosses, with a stronger major line every few lines. Colour and opacity. Coordinates: the easting and northing (or longitude and latitude) of the major lines along the top and left edges of the map, read as the map moves. Refresh (Ctrl+R, on the Navigate toolbar) draws every layer again: imagery and terrain read anew, vector layers and the network rebuilt, the Layers panel and the open attribute tables brought up to date.

The Browser tab beside Layers shows the computer's folders and the files FlowCHAOS can open (networks, projects, shapefiles, drawings, GeoPackages, KML, rasters, survey points); a shapefile's other parts are not listed. Drag a file onto the map or the Layers panel, double-click it, or right-click it and Add to Project. The list at the top goes to the drives, your folders, the project's folder and your favourites; the star keeps the folder you are in as a favourite.

FlowCHAOS keeps large projects responsive: an edit of the network does not copy the vector layers it does not touch, so moving a node is as quick with a large drawing loaded as without it; line layers are drawn as one path for each colour; shaded DEMs are worked out in the background and in limited memory; a hidden raster keeps only a small overview; and a tool window that is closed (a 3D view, a profile, the planner) gives its memory back, and opens again from the project when it is needed.
Turn survey points, network levels or a DEM into contours, colour relief, 3D surfaces and more.

The Contours button (or Add Layer > Surface Map) opens the map maker. Choose the source from the map (a point layer, an earlier surface map, a DEM or the network's node levels) or from a file, then the map type: Map type What it shows Contour map lines, optionally filled bands, with labels that read uphill Colour relief continuous colours with hill shading Post map, classed post map the points with their values or classes 3D surface, 3D wireframe the terrain in its own 3D window Point cloud the points coloured by level Peaks and depressions high and low points of the surface The surface is made in the background with a progress window. The automatic cell size is fine enough for smooth surfaces and edges (at least 250 cells across); set your own in the properties. Contour lines drawn in another program can be used directly: choose a DXF file as the source and its contour polylines (with their elevation), 3D lines and points become the points of the surface. The work is done in the background: the status bar shows the task, its progress and a Cancel button, and the map stays usable meanwhile.

A DEM is drawn as terrain: a colour for its height (greens low, yellows and browns on the slopes, grey and white on the heights) lit by a hillshade from several directions, so every slope is modelled and none is lost in shadow. Zoomed in past the cells of the data the surface stays smooth; zoomed out, each pixel shows the average of the cells under it, so there is no speckle. On gentle ground the shading is raised (the heights are not changed), so the channels and banks of a floodplain still show. Choose hillshade, colour only or grey in the layer's properties.

section: A DEM from points, contours or a surface
text: Layer > Make DEM (GeoTIFF) builds a terrain model as a GeoTIFF from data in the project: a contour or surface layer, a line layer of contours or a point layer with an elevation field, the levels of a network layer or of all junctions; or from a CSV file of points, choosing which columns hold X (easting), Y (northing) and Z. To use the contours of a DXF drawing, add the drawing as vector layers first (only its contour layer, if you like) and choose that layer. The data are read and analysed in the background, so the window keeps responding, and the settings are suggested from them: the cell size, the longest triangle side that still belongs to the survey, and the terrace correction for contours. The surface is smooth by default: it passes through every point and curves between them, with no sharp corners where the triangles meet; a flat triangulated surface (TIN) can be chosen instead. A 1 m DEM of a large scheme takes about a minute and runs in the background. The new DEM can be added to the map and, if asked, contoured at once.

Gridding method Character Kriging (linear variogram) the default: honours every point, smooth between them Minimum curvature (thin-plate spline) the smoothest surface; may overshoot between sparse points Triangulation (TIN) linear between points: exact but faceted, so contours bend at triangle edges Inverse distance to a power weighted by distance; flat spots around the points Line smoothing (None, Low, Medium, High, Very high) draws smooth contour lines: the surface is resampled finer with cubic interpolation before the lines are traced, grid-cell jitter is removed, and the corners are rounded. The lines stay on their level; Medium suits most maps, Very high gives the softest lines.

Each map type has the properties that make sense for it: gridding method and cell size, levels, fill, lines and labels for contours; colour, shading direction, smoothness, opacity and an optional contour overlay for relief; symbols for post maps; surface, light and frame for 3D. Right-click a surface map for New Map from This Source to make another type from the same data.

Double-click a 3D surface in the layers list, or use Contours > Open 3D View, to open it again at any time. Drag to turn and tilt (the surface turns the way the mouse moves), Shift-drag to pan, wheel to zoom. Preset views, vertical exaggeration, detail, light direction, walls to a base, axes with values, a colour scale, draped contours and high-resolution image export.
Contours export as DXF, Shapefile or GeoPackage; surfaces as an ASCII grid (.grd); maps go on sheets in the print layout.
Size pipes automatically, check fire flow, draw long sections and set design levels.

Analysis > Automatic Pipe Sizing finds the cheapest sizes of a pipe series that keep the network within your limits. It works in stages, each with the advanced solver: Feasibility: with every pipe at its largest size, junctions still short of pressure are limited by the source level. They are reported (a pump or a higher tank is needed) and not chased. Sizes from flows: the flows at peak demand give each pipe the smallest size that carries its flow below the velocity limit. Repair: pipes that are too fast or lose too much head go up a size; where junctions are short of pressure, the pipes on the paths that supply them go up where a size gains the most head for its extra cost. Cost reduction: each pipe is tried one size smaller, largest savings first, and kept smaller only where every limit still holds. Settings Setting Meaning Pipes to size every pipe, or the selected ones Pipe series 45 series, the most used first: HDPE PE100 and PE80 in every pressure class, uPVC by PN and by Class 6, 9, 12 and 16, PVC-O, irrigation laterals and mains, PPR, PEX, copper and galvanised steel for buildings, ductile iron, steel, GRP, asbestos cement and concrete for large mains, and North American sizes; or your own Maximum velocity no pipe may run faster Minimum pressure every junction that takes water must keep it (or every junction, if chosen) Maximum head loss per kilometre, optional Peak factor every withdrawal times this factor, to design for the peak hour Minimum velocity slower pipes are flagged (water may stagnate) Maximum pressure higher junctions are flagged (a pressure reducing valve may help) Smallest pipe no pipe below this diameter Only enlarge no pipe becomes smaller than it is (for extending a network) Reduce cost the cost reduction stage Pipes with the field size_locked = yes keep their size. A main that fills a tank is sized for the demand the tank supplies (in a steady run a tank fills as fast as its inlet allows, which is not a design flow). Results The table shows each pipe's current and new size, nominal size, flow, velocity, head loss and a note. The summary gives the cost of the design (from the series' prices, or a relative cost), lengths by size, the lowest pressure, and the pipes and junctions that need attention. Apply Sizes writes diameter, roughness, material, pressure class and nominal size in one step that can be undone. Add prices to a series to see real costs: see reference data.

Analysis > Fire Flow Analysis gives, for every hydrant, the largest flow it can deliver while its residual pressure and the pressure at every other junction stay above the minimums. Test every junction, the selected ones, or those whose hydrant field is yes. The table shows the static pressure, available flow, residual pressure and the node that limits each hydrant; Select Failing Hydrants shows on the map where the network needs strengthening. How it works: for each hydrant the fire flow is added as an extra withdrawal and the network is solved again, raising the flow until a pressure limit is reached (a search that needs only a few runs). The model stays open between runs, so even large networks finish quickly, and Stop ends the analysis at once, keeping the hydrants already tested.

Analysis > Criticality Analysis asks, for each pipe, pump or valve: what if it were out, from a burst or a repair? Each tested link is closed in turn. Junctions that lose every path to a reservoir or tank are cut off: all their withdrawal is lost. The rest of the network is solved with pressure-dependent withdrawal: a junction below the service pressure delivers only part of its withdrawal, and nothing at or below the pressure where delivery stops. What it misses beyond its normal shortfall counts as lost too. Setting Meaning Test every pipe, the selected links, or every pipe, pump and valve Smallest pipe tested skip service pipes below this diameter on large networks Service pressure full withdrawal at or above this pressure Delivery stops at no withdrawal at or below this pressure At design withdrawal demand patterns held at 1, times the peak factor; off, the patterns at the start time Each link is rated by the share of the total withdrawal not delivered while it is out: High from 20 %, Medium from 5 %, Low from 0.5 %, otherwise None. The table also shows the junctions cut off, the shortfall and the lowest pressure that remains. Double-click a row to find the link; Select High and Medium selects them all; Show on Map colours the links by criticality (the Criticality link view, kept with the project); Export CSV lists the affected junctions too. Reservoirs and tanks keep supplying for the moment analysed, so a pump that fills a tank may show no effect: the tank covers the outage until it runs down. Use an extended period run to see how long.

Select pipes and choose L-Profile (Ctrl+Shift+P). The profile shows ground, pipe invert, minimum cover and the hydraulic grade line, with tables of levels, depth, cover and chainage and the excavation quantities. It follows the selection on the map. The sheet is drawn at the Horizontal scale on screen chosen above it (1:2,000 by default; 1:500 to 1:50,000, or Fit to window) and is as long as the pipeline at that scale: it scrolls sideways, and Ctrl with the mouse wheel zooms along it. The settings are on the left; Build Profile, Export (PDF, PNG or the chainage table as CSV) and Close stay at the foot of the window. The values never overlap: where chainages crowd together they are spread apart with a leader line back to their true place, as in the planning network diagram, and node names do the same. If even that leaves no room the sheet says how many node values were left out (the CSV table has them all). Vertical exaggeration: fit the sheet, or fix it (for example 10:1) when the sheet has room. Chainage as km+m: 1+234.5 instead of 1234.5. High and low points: peaks of the pipe (for air valves) and dips (for washouts) are marked; fittings already on the map are filled, points found from the levels are open. Quantities box: in the header, in a corner of the chart, or dragged to any place on the sheet. The trench is the pipe's outside diameter plus the trench allowance wide, and reaches the bedding depth below the invert; excavation is summed along the profile from these. The grade line is drawn between every node that has a result, so a node left out of the analysis does not remove it.
Design Levels sets invert levels from the ground and a cover depth, or tank stand heights, for the selected nodes.

Design > Area Demand Allocator (also in the Irrigation menu and the Processing Toolbox) sets the design withdrawals of junctions from the polygons they supply: the blocks of an irrigation scheme, the zones of a town. The settings are on the left and the matches on the right; Match, Apply and Close stay at the foot of the window. The areas are measured from the polygons themselves (holes left out, on the ellipsoid like the areas of a GIS), in hectares, square metres, acres or square kilometres, so the layer needs no area field. The demand of each area comes from one of two bases: A rate for each unit of area (unit area loading): its area times the rate, for example the peak irrigation requirement in l/s per hectare, and a factor. A total flow shared by area: the scheme's design flow shared among the areas in proportion to their areas, times the factor. Tick Share by a number stored for each area to use a field instead of the measured area, for example a population or a number of plots (the attribute table's field calculator can work one out first). The withdrawals are rounded to the Decimal places chosen (2 by default), in the table and when set. The demand of each area goes to its junctions by one of the methods of the design literature: The junction in each area (nearest node): the junction inside it nearest its centre; with none inside, the junction nearest the area within the search distance. Shared equally among the junctions in each area (equal distribution). Each junction takes the area it lies in. Thiessen service areas: each junction supplies the part of the areas nearer to it than to any other junction (Voronoi polygons), so an area's demand is split by the share of it each junction serves. Shared by half the length of the pipes at each junction (the unit length method): a junction with more pipe around it takes a larger share of the area's demand. Match lists every area (numbered as in its layer) with its area, its withdrawal, the junction's current withdrawal, its junction (a shared area shows each junction's share) and how it was found, and draws an arrow on the map from each area to its junction, coloured by how it was found; the colours of inside, nearest outside, set by hand and no junction can be chosen. Change a match in the table, select a junction on the map and Use Selected Junction, or drag on the map: an arrow's head dropped on another junction gives the area to that junction, and an end dropped inside another area has that junction supply that area instead; the table follows. Clear the Map takes the arrows and highlights off the map. The summary counts what was found and names junctions that supply more than one area, to check. Apply replaces the design withdrawals (or adds to them), and can set the junctions that supply no area to zero; it is one step of Undo. A banner above the table says how it went: green when every junction has its new withdrawal (shown in green under Current), amber when some areas had no junction,...

The Irrigation menu holds sprinkler, drip and centre pivot design tools that start from crop water needs and soil and draw the layout on the map. Each design tool has a Concept drawing page beside its report: the field to scale with the mainline or manifold, the laterals, the sprinklers and their wetted circles or the drip rows, the blocks watered one after another, the source and pump, dimensions, a legend, a north arrow, a scale bar and a title block. Choose the land shape (rectangle, L-shaped, tapering, triangle, irregular; for a pivot a circle in a square field, a full or a half circle): every shape keeps the area of the designed field. Export it as PNG or PDF (A3); a saved report includes it. Quick Design Estimates gives a first look from a few inputs: for drip the daily need reduced for ground cover, the emitters, the application rate, the watering time and the blocks that fit the hours available; for sprinklers the depth the soil and roots hold, the interval, the precipitation rate (checked against the soil's intake), the set time, the sprinklers running together and the pump flow. Irrigation > Climate Data reads monthly climate records (.clim) for crop water needs, and Apply Climate to Withdrawals turns them into the withdrawals of the irrigated junctions. The climate window is a sheet of the twelve months: each month's reference evapotranspiration and rainfall, with the effective rainfall and the net need worked out, and the peak month marked. Type the values, or paste them from a spreadsheet or a text (tab, comma or semicolon separated, with or without a month column); New Climate Sheet starts a blank one, Save Climate File keeps it as a .clim file to use again, and Sample Data loads the Lilongwe means after asking before it replaces entries. Choose a month and FlowCHAOS scales the outlets for it; the design flow is kept with the project. Sample Projects has a sprinkler scheme in July with the Lilongwe (Chitedze) climate to try it with.
Bills of quantities measured from the design and kept with it, and the construction programme that follows them.

File > Export > Bill of Quantities (or the BOQ button) opens the BOQ Workbench in its own window. The bill is part of the project: it is saved with it, and every change can be undone from the main window. Generating a bill Generate asks for the BOQ type (water supply, irrigation, building plumbing), the contents (every section of the type with blanks to complete, or only the work found on the map), the company and client details, the regional preset (currency, tax, levies, contingency), the default pipe materials and the trench sizes. The bill is then measured from the network: pipes by material, outside diameter and pressure class (from the modelled or static pressures); fittings from the geometry: bends by angle, tees, crosses, reducers, end caps, flange adaptors; valves by type and size, chambers, air valves, washouts and hydrants; earthworks from the trench width and depth: clearing, excavation, bedding, backfill and surplus; pumps with their duty point, tanks with their volume and stands, sources and connections. Editing and tracing The bill is a tree of bills, elements and items. Double-click a description, unit, quantity, rate or note to change it; add items, elements and bills, move rows up and down, or delete them. The From column tells where each quantity comes from: From Meaning Network measured from the map Lump sum a fixed quantity To complete a provisional item: type its quantity Typed added or changed by hand Select a measured item and press Show on Map: the pipes and nodes it was measured from are selected on the map. When the network changes, Update Quantities measures it again: measured items follow, items typed by hand and every rate are kept, new work is added and work that left the network is marked. Show: Changed by the last update lists what moved. Pricing Type a rate in the Rate column. Build it up in the Item panel: materials, labour, plant and equipment and transport for one unit, plus overheads and profit; Use This Rate prices the selected items. Rates > Import Rates from a Priced Spreadsheet reads any workbook with Description and Rate columns (a contractor's priced bill, a company rate list) into the project's rate library and prices the matching items. Add This Bill's Rates to the Library keeps your rates for the next bill. Plugins can add their own rate sources (see Writing plugins). Items with a quantity but no rate are shaded; Show: Quantity but no rate lists them. Summary The Summary panel gives each bill's total, the net total, contingency, levies, tax and the grand total, the cost per kilometre of pipe and per connection, how complete the pricing is, and a chart of each bill's share of the cost. Revisions and export Revisions > Save a Revision keeps a copy (Rev A, Rev B, ...). Compare with a Revision lists every item whose quantity or rate changed and the change in the grand total; Restore a Revision brings one back. Export writes the bill as a spreadsheet (.xlsx) with the company letterhead, a docu...

Analysis > Project Planning opens the planner: a task table and a Gantt chart side by side, with drag to move, resize and link tasks; constraints, deadlines, calendars and working time; critical path, PERT probabilities, resources and levelling; baselines, progress, status date and earned value with the cost curve; schedule risk and a schedule quality check (the Risk and quality tab). Schedule risk. The plan is scheduled many times (1,000 by default) with each duration drawn at random: from the task's optimistic, most likely and pessimistic days when they are given, otherwise within a range around its duration (90 to 125 % unless you change it). The tab shows the finish date met in half the runs (P50), in 80 (P80) and in 90 (P90), the chance of finishing as planned, the spread of the finish as a chart and how often each task was on the critical path. Schedule quality check. The 14-point assessment used to judge whether a plan can be relied on: tasks without a predecessor or successor, leads, lags, links other than finish to start, hard constraints, high and negative float, long tasks, invalid progress, tasks without resources, missed tasks, a critical path that runs to the finish, the critical path length index and the baseline execution index. Each row gives what was found, the limit, Pass or Fail and the tasks concerned; checks that need a baseline, a status date or a deadline say so until they have them. Manual and automatic scheduling. An auto scheduled task takes its dates from its links, constraints and the calendar. Task > Manually Schedule pins the selected tasks to their start dates: they stay there when their predecessors move (the plan warns when a predecessor finishes later), and dragging the bar moves the pinned date. Task > Auto Schedule gives them back to the scheduler. Project > New Tasks Manually Scheduled decides how new tasks start. Manual tasks are drawn with brackets at both ends of the bar and can be listed with View > Filter > Manually Scheduled Tasks. Formatting the Gantt chart. View > Gantt Chart Style sets the theme (the colours of task, critical, summary and manual bars, milestones, progress, baseline and links, each of which can be changed), the bar shape (rounded, square, shaded or flat) and height, how progress is drawn, the text beside the bars (task names, resource names, durations, dates, percent complete) and the parts shown (links, baseline, critical path, float, non-working days, gridlines, the today and status date lines). View > Gantt Presets applies a whole format at once (Standard, Tracking, Critical path, Presentation, Detailed, Print in black and white); the themes and presets are in resources/data/planning/gantt_styles.json. The style is kept with the plan, and printed and exported charts use it. View also filters the tasks (critical, milestones, incomplete, late, manually scheduled) and shows the outline to a level. Project > Move Project moves the whole plan to a new start da...
Compose map sheets, profiles and reports for printing and sharing.

File > Export > Print Layout opens the layout designer in its own window. Pick an item on the left toolbar, then drag a rectangle on the page (or click for the default size). Item What it shows Map everything the main map shows (the network, vector layers with their labels, contours, terrain, imagery and basemaps) at a chosen scale; can follow the main map 3D Map a lit 3D view of a surface map, with axes and colour scale Picture a logo or photo Label text with fields such as {project} and {scale} Dynamic Text text filled when printed: date, time, scale, author, file, pipe length, withdrawal Legend the network symbols, vector layers (and their classes), terrain and imagery, contour layers and the result colour ramp; choose which appear and rename them Scale Bar linked to a map: alternating boxes, single box or line with ticks North Arrow classic, compass rose or triangle Shape rectangle, ellipse or line Marker a map pin, circle, square, triangle, diamond, star or cross, with a label Arrow an arrow in any direction, with heads at the end, the start or both Node Item a polyline or polygon whose points you type in millimetres HTML formatted text: headings, lists, tables and fields Attribute Table nodes or links with the columns you choose, filtered and sorted Fixed Table a table you type: revisions, notes, a title block Summary Table pipe lengths by diameter, node results or link results Elevation Profile ground, pipe and hydraulic grade along the pipes selected on the map Rulers, guides, smart snapping, alignment, rotation, locking, copy and paste, and undo help you compose. Every item has its own properties panel; the layout redraws when the network changes, and Refresh (Ctrl+R) draws every item again from the project as it is now. A legend lists what the project holds. In its properties, untick an item to leave it out, double-click one to rename it, or use Show All and Hide All. Export as PDF, image or SVG, or print. Layouts are saved with the project, and a project can hold several.

section: Moving the map inside its frame
text: Double-click a map on the page to work inside it: drag to pan the map without moving the frame, turn the wheel to zoom around the pointer. A banner says you are moving map content; Esc or another double-click returns to arranging items. The same mode is the first button of the tools bar, Move Map Content (C). Ctrl and the wheel zoom a map at any time. Locked maps keep their view. In the map's properties, Use map view takes the area shown in the main window, Whole network fits the network, and Show on main map zooms the main window to the area of this map.

A new map has no grid. A map on the sheet can carry several coordinate grids: select the map and use Grids in its properties. Add Grid adds a grid in the project's coordinates (metres); Add Latitude and Longitude Grid adds one in degrees, whose lines curve where the projection makes them curve. Tick a grid in the list to show it, choose it to change it: Draw as: lines, crosses at the intersections, dots, or none (only the frame and labels). Interval and Offset for each direction, or automatic, a round step chosen from the map's scale. Line colour, width and style, and the size of the crosses. Frame: zebra bands, ticks inside or outside the map (or both), or a line round it. Labels on the sides chosen, outside or inside the map, along the left and right edges or level, as numbers, numbers with E and N, degrees, minutes and seconds, degrees and decimal minutes or decimal degrees, with their decimals, size and colour. A metre grid labelled outside and a latitude and longitude grid labelled inside sit together without their labels meeting. Maps of layouts made before keep their edge ticks as their first grid.

A sheet can hold several maps: a detailed one and a small one of the whole study area. In the small map's properties, Show the extent of names the detailed map, and its extent is drawn as a frame on the overview (a marker when it is too small to see). The frame follows as you pan and zoom the detailed map.

Labels, dynamic text and HTML items replace these fields when drawn: {project}, {title}, {date}, {date_long}, {time}, {scale}, {crs}, {author}, {company}, {layout}, {paper}, {file}, {nodes}, {links}, {pipe_km}, {withdrawal}, {analysis} and {version}.

Long sections export as A3 PDF, PNG or a chainage table (CSV). Contour map sheets with axes, ticks and grid. Results export as spreadsheets; graphs as images. File > Export > Canvas as Image or Canvas as PDF: the map view as it is shown, every visible layer included, at print quality (PNG, JPEG, TIFF, BMP, WebP, SVG or PDF).

The FlowCHAOS network file (.fcnet): how a network is stored, part by part, so it can be shared, checked and read by other tools. A network file holds one network: its elements, demand profiles, curves, controls, rules, analysis options, units and coordinate system, and optionally the look of its layer. FlowCHAOS writes one with Export Layer As > FlowCHAOS Network and opens it with File > Open or Add Layer, as a network layer. A project file (.fchaos) holds a whole project (many layers, rasters, plans, layouts); a network file is for sharing one network or adding it to another project.

It is JSON text in UTF-8: readable in any text editor, and easy to read from a script or a spreadsheet tool. The parts always come in the same order, each with a plain name. Short lists (a point, the factors of a profile, an option) are kept on one line. Lengths are in metres, levels in metres above the datum, diameters in millimetres and flows in litres per second, unless units says otherwise; coordinates are in the coordinate_system. Every element has an id that never changes (references use it) and a name that you see on the map and that controls and rules refer to.

Part What it holds format, version flowchaos-network and the layout version (2). A newer FlowCHAOS reads older versions. about the network's name, a description, the program and version that wrote it, and when (UTC) units the unit system and the units of flow, length, diameter and pressure coordinate_system the coordinate system of every x and y, as an EPSG code (for example EPSG:32736) network the elements, in six lists: junctions, reservoirs, tanks, pipes, pumps, valves demand_profiles each profile by name: the factors of its periods, in order curves each curve by name: its kind (Pump head, Pump efficiency, Storage volume, Component loss) and its points controls simple controls, one line each rules rule-based controls, one line each (RULE, IF, AND, OR, THEN, ELSE, PRIORITY) analysis the analysis options by group (options, times, quality, energy, report and others), one entry per setting layer_style optional: the symbols, colours and labels of the layer settings optional: FlowCHAOS settings that belong to this network

Junctions, reservoirs and tanks share these fields: Field Meaning id the permanent identity of the node name the name shown on the map and used in controls and rules x, y the place, in the coordinate system of the file elevation_m the level used in the analysis (for a reservoir, its water level) demand_lps the design withdrawal (junctions) properties everything else the node has Common properties: ground_elevation_m (the ground), design_offset_m (the pipe level below or above the ground), demand_profile, base_demand_lps, emitter_coefficient, description. A tank adds initial_level_m, minimum_level_m, maximum_level_m, diameter_m, minimum_volume_m3, stand_height_m and, when it has one, volume_curve. A reservoir may have total_head_m and a demand_profile that makes its level vary through the day.

Pipes, pumps and valves share these fields: Field Meaning id, name as for nodes from, to the ids of the start and end nodes; flow is positive from from to to diameter_mm the inside diameter roughness the roughness for the friction formula of the analysis options status OPEN, CLOSED or CV (a pipe with a check valve) vertices optional: the bends between the two nodes, as x, y points properties everything else the link has Common properties: material, minor_loss, model_length_m (a length given by the source of the network, used instead of the length on the map). A pump adds pump_type and pump_parameters (its head curve, power, speed and speed profile); a valve adds valve_type (PRV, PSV, PBV, FCV, TCV or GPV) and setting.

section: Reading a network file from a script
text: The file is ordinary JSON, so any language can read it. In Python: import json with open("village.fcnet", encoding="utf-8") as stream: network = json.load(stream)["network"] for pipe in network["pipes"]: print(pipe["name"], pipe["diameter_mm"], pipe["properties"].get("material"))

For programs that do not read network files, FlowCHAOS imports and exports the hydraulic model input format (.inp, Export Layer As > Hydraulic Model). It is the format of the widely used public-domain network modelling program, not a FlowCHAOS format; FlowCHAOS supports it so models can be exchanged. That format has a fixed set of sections (junctions, reservoirs, tanks, pipes, pumps, valves, profiles, curves, controls, rules, options and times). FlowCHAOS keeps what the format cannot hold (ground levels, design offsets, materials, labels, layer styles) in the project, writes a harmless default for anything an imported model refers to but does not define, and renames names already used in the project on import (T1 becomes T1_2), with every reference to them. A project has one coordinate reference system (CRS), shown in the status bar. New projects use the default coordinate system, EPSG:32736 (UTM zone 36 South) until you choose another. On the first start FlowCHAOS suggests one for the country the computer is set to (its national grid or UTM zone); change it at any time in Settings > Default Coordinate System. How FlowCHAOS solves a network: the equations, the methods, and how time and water quality advance.

For a network of n junctions and m links, a hydraulic state is found when: at every junction i, the flows Q in and out balance the withdrawal d: sum(Q in) - sum(Q out) = d(i); along every link from node i to node j, the heads H satisfy H(i) - H(j) = h(Q), where h is the head loss of a pipe or valve, or minus the head added by a pump. The head loss of a pipe is h = r Q |Q|^(n-1) + m Q |Q|, with r from the friction formula and m from the minor losses. Because h depends on Q nonlinearly, the equations are solved by iteration.

The advanced engine, the default, uses the global gradient method (Todini and Pilati, 1988). Each iteration: Linearises every link around its current flow: h = h(Q0) + h'(Q0) (Q - Q0). Eliminates the flows, leaving a symmetric, sparse system in the unknown heads, which is solved by sparse Cholesky factorisation. Updates every flow from the new heads. Checks the status of pumps, check valves and control valves at the set frequency. Stops when the sum of the flow changes, divided by the total flow, is below the accuracy (0.001 by default), and any limits on head error and flow change are met. Continuity holds exactly after every iteration, so even an unconverged state balances at the nodes. Convergence is usually reached in 5 to 20 iterations whatever the size of the network.

Settings > Hydraulic Solver offers other algorithms, for checking a result or for teaching: Algorithm Unknowns How it works Built-in sparse Newton flows and heads Newton on the full system with least-squares safeguards; models pressure-driven withdrawal and control valves Global gradient (Todini and Pilati, 1988) flows and heads the method above, written independently Newton nodal (Martin and Peters, 1963) heads Newton on the junction heads alone, with flows from the heads; damped by a line search Linear theory (Wood and Charles, 1972) flows and heads each element made linear and the system solved exactly; flows averaged between iterations Hardy Cross (1936) loop flows one loop corrected at a time, with pseudo-loops between sources; slow, but every step can be followed by hand Analysis > Compare Solvers runs them side by side and reports the iterations, time, and the largest differences in head and flow; extended-period runs always use the advanced engine.

In a pressure-driven run each junction's withdrawal becomes an unknown that follows its pressure (see The network model). The advanced engine adds the withdrawals to its unknowns and solves them with the heads. The comparison algorithms model each withdrawal as an outlet link from the junction to a virtual reservoir at its elevation plus the minimum pressure, whose head loss reproduces the delivery curve, so every method answers the same question.

An extended period is a sequence of hydraulic states: The state at the start time is solved with the tank levels and the controls at their starting values. The time to the next event is found: the next hydraulic step, the next change of a demand profile, the time a tank would fill or empty, or the time a control or rule would act. Tank levels are advanced over that time with the flows found (each level changes by the net flow divided by the tank's area at that level). Controls and rules are evaluated; statuses change; the next state is solved. Results are reported at every report step; between them, the run can take shorter steps so a tank never overshoots its limits and a control acts at the right moment.

Water quality is solved with the hydraulics, by an event-driven Lagrangian method: each pipe holds a series of water segments of different quality; at each quality step, water enters at one end and leaves at the other, so segments move with the flow; segments whose qualities differ by less than the quality tolerance are merged; at each node, the water leaving is the flow-weighted mix of the water arriving, plus any source; reactions change each segment's concentration over the step: bulk decay at kb C^n, wall decay by a rate limited by the transfer of the substance to the wall (from the pipe diameter, velocity and diffusivity); tanks mix by their model (fully mixed, two compartments, plug flow or stacked). Short quality steps (one to five minutes) keep the results accurate; the warm-up period of a study lets the starting values wash out.

Answers to the questions engineers ask most often.

How do I model a borehole with a submersible pump? A reservoir at the pumping water level (the static level plus the drawdown at the pumped flow), then the pump from that reservoir to a node at the pump's depth, then the riser pipe to the wellhead. The sample Smallholder solar borehole, 1.5 ha drip shows it. The pump's head-flow curve must cover the lift from the pumping level to the delivery point plus the friction. How do I model a break-pressure tank? As a pressure breaker valve or, more stable in every case, as a pressure reducing valve set to about 1 m: the downstream network then starts from the tank's level. The sample Rural gravity piped scheme uses them. How do I model a float valve on a tank inlet? Let the tank close its own inlet when full (the default), or add a control: close the inlet pipe when the tank rises above a level, open it below another. How do I model leakage? With outflow coefficients (emitters) at junctions, whose outflow grows with pressure, or as an extra withdrawal category. Estimate the coefficients from the night flow of a district: the leakage at night pressure gives C = q / p^n. How do I model intermittent supply? Use a pressure-driven analysis, a demand profile that is zero when the supply is off, and controls that close the main valve during those hours. The delivered withdrawal shows who receives water. How do I model a hydrant or fire flow? Analysis > Fire Flow Analysis checks every hydrant for the required flow at the residual pressure. For one hydrant in a run, add its flow as a withdrawal at the hydrant junction. How do I model a pump that runs on solar power only in the day? A clock-time control or a rule: open at 8 AM, closed at 4 PM, and closed when the tank is full. The rule samples include Solar pumping hours with a full-tank stop.

Why are some pressures negative? The network cannot deliver the withdrawals at those junctions with the head available. In a demand-driven run the shortfall shows as negative pressure; run a pressure-driven analysis to see what each junction would actually receive, then enlarge pipes or add head. Why does my run stop with "unbalanced"? See Errors and warnings: usually a disconnected part, a pump that cannot lift, or valves set against each other. Why does my tank empty (or fill) every day? Supply and demand over the day do not match: compare the system flow graph (production against consumption), check the pump's controls and the demand profile, and the tank's size. What is the difference between design withdrawal and delivered withdrawal? The design withdrawal is what the junction asks for; the delivered withdrawal is what the run gave it. They are the same in a demand-driven run; in a pressure-driven run the delivered withdrawal is smaller where the pressure is short.

Which head loss formula should I use? Hazen-Williams is the usual choice for water supply at normal velocities; Darcy-Weisbach is the most exact for any pipe, velocity and temperature. Keep one formula for a project. What velocities and pressures should I design for? Follow your standard; common values are 0.5 to 1.5 m/s in distribution, a minimum pressure of 10 to 15 m (5 to 10 m at communal taps), and a maximum static pressure of 60 to 80 m. The project's design standard holds the values the tools start from. How do I choose pipe classes? The pipe class (PN) must exceed the highest pressure the pipe sees, static or in operation, plus an allowance for surge. Check the static pressure with the pumps off and the tanks full; in long rising mains, keep a margin for surge.

Can I use my old models? Yes: FlowCHAOS imports hydraulic model input files (.inp) and binary model files (.net) of the widely used public-domain modelling program; each becomes a network layer, with its profiles, curves, controls and rules. Save your work as a FlowCHAOS project (.fchaos) or network file (.fcnet) to keep everything. Can I work offline? Yes. Everything works offline except online basemaps, satellite imagery, place search and online terrain. Offline basemaps (MBTiles) and DEMs work without a connection. Where are my files and settings? Projects are where you save them. Settings, logs and your own reference data are listed in Install, under Where FlowCHAOS keeps things.

Is FlowCHAOS free? Yes. FlowCHAOS is freeware: it is licensed without a fee for commercial, academic and public-sector use under the FlowCHAOS Freeware Licence. Which Windows do I need? Windows 10 or later, 64-bit, with 4 GB of memory (8 GB for large networks and terrain). How do I report a problem? Help > Report an Issue, with the project and the value you expected. Calculation questions are answered first.
When something does not work as expected.

Every part of the network must be connected to a reservoir or a tank. Nodes without pipes (survey points) are left out on purpose. Check reservoir levels and tank levels: a source lower than the junctions cannot supply them. Pumps need a head curve; valves need a setting. Very small or very large values (a 1 mm pipe, a 100 km pipe) often point to a units mistake.

text: The source is too low or the pipes are too small. Run Automatic Pipe Sizing: it reports the junctions the source cannot serve whatever the sizes (a pump or a higher tank is needed there) and sizes the rest.

text: The file was read in the wrong coordinate system. Remove it and import it again with its system, or correct a raster's system in its properties.
It needs something first: point at it to see what (a selection, results, a pipe, a DEM).

text: Turn off labels and the flow animation while you work, hide layers you do not need, or show them only between two scales (Layer Properties > Display).

Open an issue with the steps, what you expected, what happened, the FlowCHAOS version (Help > About) and the last lines of the log: %LOCALAPPDATA%\FlowCHAOS\FlowCHAOS\logs\flowchaos.log. A small project that shows the problem helps the most. Suspected calculation errors are handled first.
Write your own tools for FlowCHAOS in Python: what a plugin is, how it is found, loaded and shared.

A plugin is Python code that FlowCHAOS loads at start-up (or when you enable it). It can: add commands to the Plugins menu; read the whole project: nodes, links, their values, every imported field, settings and results; change the network, as one step the user can undo; run analyses, use the design tools and read their results; open its own windows and dialogs with Qt (PySide6); add tools to the Processing Toolbox, with parameters, help, a log and a result table; add rate sources to the BOQ Workbench (a rate database, a supplier's price list); read and write files: reports, exports, imports from your own formats. Plugins are grouped by what they add: GIS (data sources, formats, map tools), CAD (drawing and editing tools), Optimisation (design and operation optimisation), Reporting (reports and exports), Cost estimation (rates and estimates) and Engineering tools (any other calculation).

A plugin is a folder with a manifest and an entry point: pipe_report/ plugin.json __init__.py plugin.json describes it: { "id": "pipe-report", "name": "Pipe Report", "description": "Length of pipe by diameter, as a table you can copy.", "version": "1.0.0", "category": "Reporting", "min_flowchaos": "0.15.0", "startup": true } Key Meaning id unique, lower case letters, digits, - and _, starting with a letter or digit name shown in the Plugins panel and menus description one sentence shown in the Plugins panel version your version number category GIS, CAD, Optimisation, Reporting, Cost estimation, Engineering tools or Other min_flowchaos the oldest FlowCHAOS version it works with (an older one refuses to load it) startup true to load it when FlowCHAOS starts (the user can switch it off) __init__.py defines register(host), called once when the plugin loads: def register(host): def run(): project = host.document.project ... host.add_plugin_action("Pipe Report", run, "Length of pipe by diameter") An optional unregister(host) is called when the plugin is switched off. Everything added through the host (commands, toolbox tools, rate sources) is removed automatically.

A tool declares its parameters; the toolbox builds its window, runs it as one undoable step when it changes the network, shows its message and table, and selects what it returns on the map: from flowchaos.core.processing import Algorithm, Outcome, Param def long_pipes(project, values, context): limit = values["limit"] rows, select = [], set() for link in project.links: if link.link_type == "PIPE" and project.link_length_m(link) > limit: rows.append([link.name, round(project.link_length_m(link), 1)]) select.add(("link", link.id)) return Outcome(f"{len(rows)} pipes longer than {limit:g} m.", ["Pipe", "Length (m)"], rows, select=select) def register(host): host.add_toolbox_algorithm(Algorithm( "my_long_pipes", "Find long pipes", "My tools", "tb-plugin", "Selects the pipes longer than the limit.", (Param("limit", "Longer than", "number", 500.0, suffix=" m"),), long_pipes, needs="links")) changes=True makes the run an undoable edit of the project; parameter kinds are number, integer, choice (with options), bool, text and file. A new group gets its own heading.

text: def register(host): def supplier_prices(boq): return {"Supply, lay, joint and test 110 mm OD uPVC PN10 pipe": 18.40} # description -> rate host.add_rate_source("Supplier price list", supplier_prices) The BOQ Workbench lists it under Rates; matching items without a rate are priced from it.

Plugins > Manage Plugins lists the installed plugins with their version, author and description. Its buttons install a plugin from a ZIP file, open the Plugin Builder (a form that writes a new plugin with the parts you choose, ready to edit), reload the plugins after you change one, open the plugin folder and uninstall the selected plugin. A sample, the Design Check Report, is in docs/plugins and the tutorial Build a plugin walks through writing one.

Location For %USERPROFILE%\.flowchaos\plugins\<id>\ your own plugins (copy the folder here) flowchaos/plugins_builtin/<id>/ plugins shipped with FlowCHAOS The Plugins panel lists every plugin, switches them on and off, installs a plugin from a .zip archive (one folder with one plugin.json) and removes user plugins.

Watch the log (%LOCALAPPDATA%\FlowCHAOS\FlowCHAOS\logs\flowchaos.log): a plugin's Python errors are written there. Create the folder in %USERPROFILE%\.flowchaos\plugins\ and restart FlowCHAOS. After a change, switch the plugin off and on again in the Plugins panel to load the new code. Errors while loading are shown in the Plugins panel and written to the log; FlowCHAOS keeps running. Keep calculations in plain functions that take a project and return values: they are easy to test with pytest without opening a window.

Change the project through host.document.apply, never directly: the change is undoable, saved and every view refreshes. See the plugin API. Long work on a worker thread: use flowchaos.core.workers.submit and update the window when it finishes, so the map stays responsive. Plain, clear text in your commands and messages. Store your plugin's settings in project.settings["plugin:<id>"] when they belong to the project, or in QSettings when they are personal.

Zip the plugin folder (the zip contains pipe_report/plugin.json and pipe_report/__init__.py) and share it. Others install it from the Plugins panel. Plugins for everyone can be proposed for plugins_builtin through a pull request.

Design tables are JSON files under flowchaos/resources/data/: pipe series for automatic sizing (design/pipe_series.json), regional settings and rates for quantities, irrigation tables. Each file starts with a _help entry explaining its fields. Tutorial: build a FlowCHAOS plugin step by step, from an empty folder to a ZIP your colleagues install. This tutorial builds Design Check Report, a plugin that lists, after a run, every pressure, velocity and head loss outside your design limits, in a window of its own and as a tool in the Processing Toolbox. The finished plugin comes with FlowCHAOS as an example (FlowCHAOS-Design-Check-1.0.0.zip); building it yourself shows every part a plugin can have. You need FlowCHAOS and a text editor; Python knowledge helps but each step shows the full code.
